NAMES.i: English needs two words for this; Sanskrit and most Indian languages have one.

NAMES.m: The light of the autumn full moon
NAMES.i: Not just any moonlight — the clear light of the autumn full moon, when the classical Kaumudi festival was held.
The water-lily that opens to the moon, as the day-lotus opens to the sun — an old image for someone who comes alive at night.
Literally "marked with a hare" — where others see a man in the moon, Indian tradition sees a rabbit.
From yāma, the night-watch — the night as something kept and watched through.
Ushas, the dawn goddess, is praised in more than twenty hymns of the Rigveda — one of its most beautiful figures.
Aruna is the charioteer of the Sun — the red that arrives before the light does.

NAMES.src: Also the name of the astronomer Varahamihira (6th century)

NAMES.i: Literally "the joining" — the moment where day meets night, treated as sacred and marked by prayer.
In classical poetics, the particular glow beauty takes on when a person is loved.
Savitri followed Death himself and argued him into returning her husband Satyavan.
Love as dyeing: the root means "to color". The heart slowly takes on the tint of the beloved, the way cloth does.
Literally "saltiness" — not perfect features, but the savour over them that makes a face alive.

NAMES.src: Wife of the sage Atri; also Shakuntala's friend in Kalidasa

NAMES.i: Offered wealth, she asked her husband Yajnavalkya instead: "Will it make me immortal?" His answer is one of the great passages of the Upanishads.
A philosopher who questioned Yajnavalkya in a royal debate so hard he warned her to stop before her head fell off.
One of the few women whose own verses survive in the Rigveda.
A boy who went to the house of Death, waited three days, and refused every gift until Death told him what happens after dying.
Asked his lineage, he told the teacher the plain truth that he didn't know his father — and was accepted for his honesty.
Sanskrit counts six seasons, not four — including a season of rains and one just before winter.

NAMES.m: Priest who performs rites at the right season

NAMES.i: In Sanskrit poetics, the meaning a poem suggests beyond what it says — held to be the soul of poetry.

NAMES.src: Rigveda — a goddess of speech and nourishment

NAMES.m: The Malaya hills; the spring breeze
NAMES.i: In old poetry, the sandal-scented wind from the Malaya hills is what stirs love in spring.
In Kalidasa's Meghaduta, an exiled lover sends a cloud as a messenger to his wife.

NAMES.src: Shravan Kumar, the devoted son in the Ramayana

NAMES.i: A bird said to live only on moonbeams — the old image of a lover who can't stop looking at the beloved's face.

NAMES.src: Heroine of Bhavabhuti's play Malatimadhava (8th century)

NAMES.i: A powerfully fragrant flower — and in one legend, cursed by Shiva never to be offered to him for telling a lie.
Old poets said the bakula tree would only flower if a woman sprinkled it with wine from her mouth.
The ashoka tree was said to burst into bloom at the touch of a beautiful woman's foot.

NAMES.m: The great river of the south

NAMES.i: The river Ganga, called "daughter of Jahnu" — the sage who swallowed her and released her through his ear.

NAMES.src: Mahabharata — the archer to whom Krishna speaks the Bhagavad Gita
Isha Upanishad takes its name from its first word

NAMES.i: Often translated "illusion", but the older sense is the power that makes the one appear as many.
The idea that the world was made not out of need but for the joy of play.

NAMES.src: Wife of Kamadeva, the god of love

NAMES.i: She chose King Nala over the gods themselves, and later found him again when he was lost and disguised.

NAMES.src: Rigveda 10.95 — the dialogue of Pururavas and Urvashi

NAMES.i: Abandoned as a baby and sheltered by birds — hence her name.
The rainy month of swings, green bangles and songs of longing for someone far away.
The word sounds like what it describes — light rain pattering on and on.
A native Telugu word, not borrowed from Sanskrit — moonlight mattered enough to get its own name.

NAMES.m: Tender new leaves; a song's refrain
NAMES.i: In Carnatic music the pallavi is the opening line a song keeps coming back to.
A flower so delicate that Kalidasa used it as the measure of softness.
Also the word for moon in Malayalam.
In Tamil poetry the soft wind from the south carries love — and restlessness with it.

NAMES.m: A flower that blooms once in twelve years
NAMES.i: In ancient Tamil poetry each landscape stands for a mood of love. The kurinji hills stand for lovers meeting.
The yazh was an ancient Tamil harp, played in the Sangam age and lost for centuries.

NAMES.src: Ilango Adigal, author of the Tamil epic Silappadikaram

NAMES.i: Naming a child after the language itself — an old gloss for the word is "sweetness".
A girl of the hill tribes who guarded millet fields — and whom the god Murugan courted in disguise.
Tamil poets compared lovely eyes to the darting kayal fish; it was also the emblem of the Pandya kings.
It blooms after dark and drops at dawn, carpeting the ground white and orange — the flower of autumn and Durga Puja in Bengal.
The shell that makes the pearl.

NAMES.src: Heroine of Tagore's Nastanirh, filmed by Satyajit Ray

NAMES.m: Where the river meets the sea

NAMES.i: From jon, moon. Jonaki was also the magazine that began modern Assamese literature.
From het, the Gujarati word for affection.
In Sikh practice, the meditative remembering of God's name.

NAMES.src: Heer Ranjha, Waris Shah's 18th-century Punjabi love epic

NAMES.i: Literally "night-moisture" — what the night leaves behind.
Born fully grown from the head of Zeus. The city of Athens carries her name.

NAMES.m: Goddess of the hunt and the wild
NAMES.i: Twin of Apollo, protector of wild animals and of girls growing up.

NAMES.m: God of music, light and healing
Queen of the underworld, bringer of spring
NAMES.i: Each year she returns from the underworld and her mother Demeter lets the earth bloom again.
When her daughter was taken, she searched the whole earth, and nothing grew until she found her.
In Hesiod she is the first to come out of Chaos, and mother of the sky itself.
Homer calls her "rosy-fingered Dawn" again and again.
Even Zeus was said to fear her.
He drives the sun across the sky in a chariot of fire.
A Titaness in Hesiod, and the grandmother of Apollo and Artemis.
A Titaness, mother of the Sun, the Moon and the Dawn.
Muse of epic poetry — Hesiod names her the greatest of the nine Muses.
Muse of history.
A giant hunter, set in the sky as the constellation you can still find each winter.
The Trojan prince who fought to protect his city; his farewell to his wife and baby son is one of the Iliad’s most tender scenes.
She could see the future truly, but was cursed so that no one would believe her.
She gave Theseus the thread that led him out of the Labyrinth. Her crown became a constellation.
Running from Apollo, she became a laurel tree — which is why victors are crowned with laurel.
A mountain nymph who could only repeat the last words spoken to her.
Rescued from a sea monster by Perseus; she is now a constellation, and a galaxy.
A mortal who won back the god of love after impossible trials, and was made immortal.
Goddess of the home fire. She received the first offering at every meal.
The gentlest of the winds, who brings spring.
The pure air the gods breathed, above the clouds.
Ancient Greek had two words for time: chronos, time passing, and kairos, the moment that matters.
For the ancient Greeks, welcoming a stranger was a sacred duty — the gods might be in disguise.
A sea nymph in Ovid; later the name of the statue that came to life.
He carried his old father on his back out of burning Troy.
Founder and queen of Carthage, who loved Aeneas.
At an omen, her hair seemed to catch fire without burning.
Virgil says she could run over a field of wheat without bending a single stalk.

NAMES.m: Roman goddess of the moon and hunt

NAMES.i: Her festival, the Floralia, celebrated spring in ancient Rome.
She cared only for her orchards, until the god of the seasons won her by disguising himself as an old woman.
She and her husband fed two strangers who turned out to be gods; their wish was to die at the same moment, and they became two trees growing side by side.
Husband of Baucis — together, an oak and a linden.
He has two faces, one looking back and one forward; January is named for him.
June is named for her.
Etruscan is a lost language, known mostly from short inscriptions. Thesan appears on bronze mirrors, bringing the morning.
She knows every person’s fate, but never tells.
Thursday is his day.
The brightest and most loved of the gods; his death begins the end of the world.
When Loki cut off her golden hair, dwarves forged her new hair of real gold.
She skis and hunts in the mountains, and chose her husband by looking only at his feet.
In Norse myth the sun is a woman, driving her chariot just ahead of a chasing wolf.
The sun’s brother, who guides the moon.
Runes are carved on his tongue.

NAMES.m: God of the sea and wind

NAMES.i: He put his hand in the wolf’s mouth so the gods could bind it, and lost it. Tuesday is his day.
The gods found two pieces of driftwood on the shore and made the first people: Ask and Embla.
A valkyrie who slept in a ring of fire until a hero rode through it.
Still an Icelandic girl’s name today.
Hild of Whitby led a great abbey and encouraged Cædmon, the first named English poet.
Also a lost letter of the English alphabet, ƿ, which stood for the w sound.
The monk Bede wrote that the English named a spring month after her — the word Easter may come from it.
Daughter of Æthelflæd, and briefly ruler of Mercia herself.
The Lady of the Mercians, who led armies and built towns in the 900s.
Deirdre of the Sorrows, who ran away with the man she loved rather than marry a king.
She was said to have the six gifts of womanhood, including wisdom, a sweet voice and fine speech.
Turned into a butterfly by a jealous rival, she was blown across Ireland for a thousand years and born again.
On the night of her betrothal to old Fionn, she ran away with young Diarmuid.
He had a love-spot on his forehead that made anyone who saw it fall in love with him.
He dreamed of a girl, searched a year for her, found her as a swan, and became a swan himself to fly with her.
The swan-maiden Aengus found.
His four children were turned into swans for nine hundred years.
The eldest of the Children of Lir, who sheltered her brothers under her wings.
Mistreated in Ireland, she trained a starling to carry a letter across the sea to her brother.
A woman made by magic from the flowers of oak, broom and meadowsweet.
Her castle is the Northern Crown, a ring of stars.
White flowers sprang up wherever she walked.
Legendary poet who swallowed three drops of wisdom and was reborn knowing everything.
A love potion drunk by mistake binds her to Tristan for life.
She lived in a tower weaving the world she saw in a mirror.
Arthur’s queen. "Jennifer" comes from the Cornish form of her name.
The old sage of the Kalevala, whose songs could calm the sea.
At the end of the Kalevala, she eats a lingonberry and bears a son who becomes king.
In Baltic songs she crosses the sky in a copper-wheeled carriage and sinks each night into the sea.
She decides each child’s fate at birth.

NAMES.m: Sea goddess of the amber palace
NAMES.i: She fell in love with a fisherman. When her palace was destroyed, its pieces became the amber that washes up on the Baltic shore.
The name became popular after Vasily Zhukovsky’s 1813 ballad "Svetlana".
Vasilisa the Wise outwits the witch Baba Yaga in Russian fairy tales.
The old bard who names the heroes and plays the kopuz in every tale.
She would only marry a man who could beat her at riding, archery and wrestling. Bamsı Beyrek did.
She rode out and fought beside Kan Turalı to save him.

NAMES.m: Legendary ancestor of the Oghuz Turks

NAMES.i: The Turkish form of Jonah, and also the Turkish word for dolphin. Yunus Emre was a beloved 13th-century poet.
An Old Turkic word carved in the 8th-century Orkhon stones — the oldest Turkic writing we have.
From kut, the old Turkic idea of heaven-given good fortune.
After Manas dies, she saves their son and raises him in secret.
His epic is still sung by bards across Tibet and Mongolia, sometimes for days at a time.

NAMES.m: The great hero of the Shahnameh

NAMES.i: Father and son met in battle without knowing each other — the saddest story in the Book of Kings.
She let down her long hair from her tower as a rope for her beloved Zal to climb.
Born with white hair, he was abandoned on a mountain and raised by the Simurgh, a great mythical bird.
Accused falsely, he rode through a mountain of fire to prove his innocence, and came out unburned.
He raised his leather apron on a spear as a banner and led the people against a tyrant.

NAMES.m: After Mithra, god of light and promises
NAMES.i: The ancient god of covenants and daylight; in Iran today, Mitra is a girl’s name.
Also a month of the Persian calendar.
He searched the ends of the earth for a way to live forever, and learned instead how to live.
Made from clay, raised among animals — and the friend whose death changed Gilgamesh.
She tells Gilgamesh to fill his belly, dance, wash, and hold a child’s hand — that is what life is for.
A wise goddess who reads her son’s dreams.
Goddess of love and war, who went down into the underworld and came back.

NAMES.m: Goddess of love and the morning star

NAMES.i: Priestess of Ur around 2300 BCE — the first author in history whose name we know.
Scribes ended their tablets with "Praise be to Nisaba".
She searched the whole of Egypt for her husband Osiris and brought him back to life.
Queen of Egypt around 1350 BCE; her painted bust is one of the most famous faces from the ancient world.
Great wife of Ramesses II, whose tomb is painted with stars.

NAMES.m: Goddess of love, music and joy

NAMES.i: At death, a heart was weighed against her feather.
She arches over the earth, and swallows the sun each evening to give birth to it each morning.

NAMES.m: Cat goddess of home and joy

NAMES.i: He sails across the sky in a boat by day and through the underworld by night.
She took up her drum and led the women in song after crossing the sea.
"Where you go, I will go" — she stayed with her mother-in-law when she could have left.
A judge and prophet who sat under a palm tree to settle disputes, and sang a victory song.
Praised for her good sense, she stopped a battle with gifts and wise words.
Swallowed by a great fish, and given a second chance.
Carried up to heaven in a chariot of fire.
"Talitha koum" — "little girl, get up" — words kept in the original Aramaic in the Gospel of Mark.
A woman in Acts remembered for her kindness and the clothes she made for others.

NAMES.m: Shining in heaven; the sun goddess
NAMES.i: When she hid in a cave, the world went dark — until the goddess Uzume danced so wildly that the gods’ laughter drew her out.
From Konohanasakuya-hime, goddess of Mount Fuji and of the cherry blossom.
Her dance brought the sun back into the world.

NAMES.m: She who invites; creator of Japan

NAMES.i: She drank the elixir of immortality and floated up to live on the moon with a jade rabbit.

NAMES.m: The goddess who mended the sky
NAMES.i: When the sky cracked, she melted stones of five colours to patch it.
When ten suns rose at once and scorched the earth, he shot down nine.

NAMES.m: The weaver girl; the star Vega
NAMES.i: Parted from the cowherd she loves by the Milky Way, she may cross it only once a year, on a bridge of magpies.
Cast away at birth, she still journeyed to the underworld to fetch the water that saved her parents, and became the guide of souls.
A bear who stayed a hundred days in a cave eating only garlic and mugwort, and became the mother of Korea’s founder.

NAMES.m: Founder of the first Korean kingdom
Maya goddess of the moon and weaving
Blood Moon; mother of the Hero Twins
NAMES.i: She spoke with a skull in a tree of the underworld, and escaped to bear the twins who defeated its lords.
He and his twin beat the lords of the underworld at their own ball game, then rose as the sun and moon.

NAMES.m: Flower-feather; goddess of beauty and flowers

NAMES.i: Carried by Túpac Amaru, the last Inca ruler, and by the rebel Túpac Amaru II.

NAMES.m: Goddess who lives in the moon
NAMES.i: Tired of her work, she climbed the rainbow to the moon — and you can still see her there, beating bark cloth.
He snared the sun to make the days longer and fished islands up from the sea.

NAMES.m: The girl who swam to her love
NAMES.i: Forbidden to meet him, she swam across Lake Rotorua at night, guided by the sound of his flute.
He pushed his parents, Sky and Earth, apart so light could come into the world.
Ranginui, the sky father, who still weeps rain for the earth mother below.

NAMES.m: Orisha of rivers, love and sweetness
NAMES.i: The orishas are living, sacred figures in Yoruba religion and its descendants in the Americas. In Yoruba families her name often appears inside longer names.
Sacred in Yoruba religion; she rules the winds and the marketplace.
Unable to walk as a child, he stood up on an iron rod that bent under him — and went on to found the Mali Empire.
Queen Amina of Zazzau led armies in the 1500s and is said to have built the city walls still called by her name.
With her twin Lisa, the sun, she made the world in Fon tradition.
Found as a baby in a ploughed furrow, she was called a daughter of the Earth.
Born from a sacrificial fire, she questioned a whole royal court when they wronged her.

NAMES.m: A name of the goddess Parvati
Heroine of the Tale of the Anklet
NAMES.i: When her husband was wrongly executed, she proved his innocence with her anklet — and her grief burned the city of Madurai.
The great dancer of the Tale of the Anklet.
A central Buddhist practice: wishing all beings well, starting with yourself.
The Buddha woke to the truth under a fig tree, called the Bodhi tree.
In Korean the same sound means "one" — two neighbours, one sound, two meanings.
The blossoms last about a week, and are loved partly because they fall so soon — a feeling Japanese calls mono no aware.
The hollyhock leaf was the family crest of the Tokugawa shoguns.
A native Korean word. In Japanese the same sound means "flower".
A native Korean word, not built from Chinese characters.
A native Korean word.
At the Mid-Autumn Festival families gather to look at the full moon together.
An old saying credited to Confucius praises the orchid for being fragrant even where no one is there to notice.
The character is made of sun (日) and moon (月) side by side.
From sar, moon, and gerel, light.
Yellow mai blossoms fill homes in southern Vietnam for Tết, the lunar new year.
Also part of hiếu thảo, devotion to one’s parents.
Jasmine garlands are the flower of Mother’s Day in Thailand.
Also the Tagalog goddess of the stars.
The same word also means "expensive" — something precious.
From Sanskrit devī — one of many words that travelled from India to the islands.
From Sanskrit putrī, daughter.
The word means ocean across many Polynesian languages, from Hawaiian to Māori.
The only palm native to mainland Aotearoa New Zealand.
The story of Layla and Majnun — the poet driven mad with love for her — is told from Arabia to Persia to India.
The word came into Arabic from Persian, and from Arabic into English and Spanish.
Literally the friend you stay up talking with after dark.
In tradition, the name of a gate of paradise for those who fasted.
Gibraltar is named after a Tariq: Jabal Tariq, "Tariq’s mountain".

NAMES.src: Nizami’s Khosrow and Shirin, a 12th-century Persian romance

NAMES.i: Arash the Archer put all his life into one arrow; where it landed became the border of Iran.
The word travelled from Sanskrit nīlotpala into Persian, then through Arabic into Spanish as nenúfar.
One of five sisters in the Book of Numbers who won the right to inherit their father’s land.
In the Book of Ruth, her daughter-in-law refuses to leave her: "where you go, I will go."
Said "Jahn" — the Turkish c sounds like an English j.
Protector of mothers and newborns in old Turkic belief.
She brought Christianity to Georgia in the 4th century, carrying a cross of vine bound with her own hair — so the story goes.
Georgia’s great 12th-century ruler, crowned with the title of king.

NAMES.m: After the medieval city of Ani
NAMES.i: Once called "the city of a thousand and one churches".
Addis Ababa means "new flower".

NAMES.m: Queen of Sheba in Ethiopian tradition
NAMES.i: In the Kebra Nagast she travels to meet King Solomon and returns to found a dynasty.
Given to a girl born soon after a grandmother has died — the family’s way of saying she has come back to them.
In Akan tradition every child has a day name for the weekday they were born on, each with its own character. It is often the first name a baby receives.

NAMES.m: Mother of rain; born in the rain
NAMES.i: Where rain is scarce it is a blessing, so a child born in the rain is a lucky one.
Niamh of the golden hair rode out of the sea to carry Oisín away to Tír na nÓg, the land of youth.
He came home from Tír na nÓg after what felt like three years — and found three hundred had passed.
Fionn mac Cumhaill burned his thumb cooking the Salmon of Knowledge — and knew everything from then on.
Goddess and saint at once; her cross of woven rushes is still made on 1 February.
In the Mabinogion she rides a white horse that no one can catch, however fast they chase.
Dylan of the Mabinogion took to the sea as soon as he was born.
A granite island in the Firth of Clyde that gives most of the world’s curling stones.
Norse goddess of love, who rode in a chariot pulled by cats.
Leif Erikson reached North America around the year 1000.
The Norse gods stayed young by eating the apples she kept.
In the Kalevala he forged the dome of the sky.
A rock on the Rhine where, in the old poems, a golden-haired woman sings boatmen onto the rocks.

NAMES.src: Dante’s guide through Paradise in the Divine Comedy

NAMES.i: One of the nine Muses — the Muse of comedy.
He swam the Hellespont every night, guided by the lamp of Hero.
The goddess who carried messages along the rainbow.
She waited twenty years for Odysseus, weaving by day and unpicking by night to keep her suitors at bay.
In legend, Rhea Silvia was the mother of Romulus and Remus.
Nadia is the everyday short form.
Invented by the poet Mihály Vörösmarty in the 1820s, from csillag, star.
The Inca sun god. Inti Raymi, the festival of the sun, is still held in Cusco every June.
Mama Killa was the Inca moon mother.
A Nahuatl name still widely given in Mexico.
A Mapuche name given in Chile and Argentina.
In Brazilian legend, a river spirit who sings from the water.

NAMES.m: Moon, silver lamp of the night sky
NAMES.i: In the traditional Hawaiian lunar calendar, every night of the moon's cycle has its own name, and farmers and fishers planted, sailed, and fished by them. To name a child Mahina is to give her the steady, guiding light that kept generations of islanders in rhythm with land and sea.
NAMES.src: Hawaiian oral tradition and lunar calendar (Kaulana Mahina)

NAMES.m: Power of the ocean, bright as a diamond
NAMES.i: Kaimana joins kai (sea) with mana (spiritual power), and it is also the Hawaiian word for diamond. Kaimana Hila, 'Diamond Head', is the crater that watches over Waikīkī, a name that holds both the sparkle and the strength of the sea.

NAMES.m: Star of gladness, Arcturus the joyful guide
NAMES.i: Hōkūleʻa is the Hawaiian name for Arcturus, the star that passes directly over the islands and served as a beacon for Polynesian navigators. In 1976 a voyaging canoe of the same name sailed from Hawaiʻi to Tahiti using only traditional wayfinding, and it revived an ancient art of the stars.

NAMES.m: Mist of heaven, soft cloud-veil of the sky
NAMES.i: Noelani combines noe (mist) with lani (heaven), an image of the soft clouds that drift down the Hawaiian mountains and shroud the ridgelines in the morning. Hawaiian poetry often treats mist as the breath of the land, gentle and sacred.

NAMES.m: Cool breeze drifting down from the mountains
NAMES.i: Keanu comes from ke anu, 'the coolness', and is often rendered as a cool mountain breeze. It evokes the relief of trade-wind air on a warm Hawaiian afternoon, a gentle presence that calms everything it touches.

NAMES.m: Mother whose children are the fish
NAMES.i: The name comes from Yeye Omo Eja, 'mother whose children are fish'. Yemoja is the orisha of the Ogun river and the ocean, and a protector of mothers and children. Her waters are said to hold the memory of every birth.

NAMES.m: King of the white cloth, lord of purity and peace
NAMES.i: Obatala, 'king of the white cloth', is the orisha of clarity, patience and moral purity. In the Ife creation story he was sent down from the sky to shape the earth and mold human bodies from clay. His devotees dress in white to honor him.
NAMES.src: Yoruba creation narratives; Ifa oral tradition

NAMES.m: Witness of destiny, sage who knows heaven's plan
NAMES.i: Orunmila is the orisha of wisdom and the patron of Ifa divination. He was present when each soul chose its destiny before birth. The name is often read as 'heaven knows who will be saved'.

NAMES.m: Beloved of God, one whom the Lord loves
NAMES.i: A traditional Yoruba name from Oluwa fe mi, 'God loves me'. It is given to a child seen as a sign of divine affection, and families often shorten it to Femi. It is used for both boys and girls.

NAMES.m: Cherished one, sweetly adored by all
NAMES.i: Aduke is an affectionate Yoruba name meaning 'one who is sweet to be cared for'. It belongs to the oruko abiso, names given to express a family's tenderness toward a child. It suits a baby who is doted on.
From Fo-ola-sade, 'honor confers the crown'. It is traditionally given in families with royal or titled lineage, where status is seen as something one grows into. It is often shortened to Sade.

NAMES.m: Child born to kin, one of the family
NAMES.i: Omolara means 'a child who is kin' and it says that the baby belongs to the whole family. In Yoruba life a child is raised by the extended lineage, not only by its parents. The name celebrates that belonging.

NAMES.m: Father returned, ancestor reborn in the child
NAMES.i: Babatunde, 'father has returned', is given to a boy born soon after a grandfather or other male elder has died. It reflects the Yoruba belief in reincarnation within the family line. Its counterpart for girls is Yetunde or Yewande.

NAMES.m: Crown, a royal gift of honor
NAMES.i: Sade means 'crown' and is a short form of Folasade and Adesola. It was made familiar to many through the singer Sade Adu, whose father was Yoruba. The Yoruba pronunciation begins with a soft 'sh' sound.

Oluwaseun means 'God has done it', and the name is a statement of gratitude. Parents give it after a long wait or a prayer answered. It is used widely across Nigeria and the diaspora, often shortened to Seun.

NAMES.m: Thunder king, lord of lightning and justice
NAMES.i: Shango is the orisha of thunder and lightning, remembered as the third king of Oyo. Tradition says he wields a double-headed axe and upholds justice and truth. His devotees honor him with drumming and dance.

NAMES.m: Healer of the forest, keeper of herbs
NAMES.i: Osanyin is the orisha of herbal medicine and the forest's healing power. Tradition says he holds the secrets of every leaf, and no remedy works without his consent. His emblem is a staff topped with a bird and ringed with iron branches.
NAMES.src: Odu Ifa corpus; Yoruba herbalist tradition

NAMES.m: Gift sought in prayer, a girl we asked for
NAMES.i: Abeni means 'we asked for her and behold, we received her'. It is an abiso name, given to a girl born after the family prayed for a child. The name carries the joy of an answered prayer.

NAMES.m: Owner of the deep ocean, lord of hidden wealth
NAMES.i: Olokun, from Oni-okun 'owner of the sea', is the orisha of the ocean's depths. Benin and Yoruba traditions describe a palace beneath the waves filled with riches and ancestral memory. Olokun is seen as either male or female depending on the region.

NAMES.m: Prince, a noble child of kings
NAMES.i: Maghan is the royal title in the name of Naré Maghan, Sundiata's father, the wise king of Mande. He listened to the hunter's prophecy and welcomed a buffalo-woman into his house.

Fakoli Koroma was the blacksmith-warrior and nephew of the sorcerer-king Sumanguru. After being wronged by his uncle, he crossed over to Sundiata's side and helped win the battle of Kirina. The smith's hammer is a sacred craft in Mande culture.

NAMES.m: Balafon, the singing wooden voice of the griot
NAMES.i: Balla Fasseke was Sundiata's griot, the keeper of his memory and the first of the Kouyaté line. The name evokes the bala, the Mande xylophone, whose gourds hum when the bard remembers the old kings.
Tiramakhan Traoré was Sundiata's celebrated commander, who in Gambian Mandinka tradition led the Mande people west toward the Atlantic. He is honored as a founder of kingdoms.
NAMES.src: Sundiata epic; Gambian Mandinka oral tradition

NAMES.i: Mande Bori, also called Manding Bory, was Sundiata's younger half-brother who shared his exile and fought beside him. He is remembered for brotherly loyalty in the long years away from Mande.

NAMES.m: Lion, a noble and courageous heart
NAMES.i: Jata (also Djata or Jara) is the Mande word for lion, and it forms the core of Sundiata's name. Griots invoke the lion as the emblem of kingly courage.

NAMES.m: Royal lineage of the lion kings of Mali
NAMES.i: Keita is the clan name of Sundiata and the emperors of Mali. It is now borne by many Mande families, who regard it as a name of royal heritage.

NAMES.m: King, a ruler of wise and generous reign
NAMES.i: Mansa is the Mande title for an emperor, as in Mansa Musa and Mansa Sundiata. Parents give it as a hope for a child of dignity and generosity.

NAMES.m: Hunter, a keeper of the wild's wisdom
NAMES.i: The donso are the Mande hunters, who are also seers and healers. In the epic, a hunter's prophecy brought Sogolon to the king, setting Sundiata's destiny in motion.

NAMES.m: Path, a bright road to destiny
NAMES.i: Sira means road or path in Mande languages. It stands for the long journey of exile and return that shapes Sundiata's story, and for finding one's own way.
NAMES.src: Mande language tradition; Sundiata epic motifs

NAMES.m: Gold, a treasure of the Mande land
NAMES.i: Sanu is the Mande word for gold, the wealth of the Mali Empire that drew traders across the Sahara. Mansa Musa's gold became legendary, and the name also lives on as the surname Sanou.

NAMES.m: Great river that flows through the Mande heartland
NAMES.i: Joliba is the Mande name for the Niger, the river that nourished the Mali Empire. Griots sing of its waters as the lifeblood of the Mande world.

NAMES.m: Singer of memory and keeper of ancestral stories
NAMES.i: The jeli, or griot, is the Mande bard who carries genealogies, epics, and the history of kings. Balla Fasseke, who narrated Sundiata's life, is the model of this role.

NAMES.m: Love, the tenderness between kin and friends
NAMES.i: Kanu is the Mandinka word for love and is given as a name in the Gambia and nearby regions. It evokes the loyalty that bound Sundiata's family and followers.

NAMES.m: Harp-lute of twenty-one strings, voice of the griots
NAMES.i: The kora is the great West African harp-lute of Mande griots, made from a calabash and strung with twenty-one strings. Its cascading notes accompany epics like Sundiata's.
Nyéléni is a figure in Bambara and Mande tradition, a woman farmer who feeds her community through hard work and wisdom. Her name has become a symbol of nourishment and the dignity of the soil.

NAMES.m: Water spirit, the creator-power of the river
NAMES.i: Faro is the Bambara and Mande spirit of water, associated with creation, order, and the Niger's flow. Mande cosmology honors him as the one who shaped the world with the word.

NAMES.m: Radiant sun-spirit of strength and daylight
NAMES.i: Lisa is the male aspect of the divine pair Mawu-Lisa, linked to the sun, heat, and the vigor of day. He balances Mawu's moonlit calm, and together they hold the world in harmony.

NAMES.m: Opener of the gate, keeper of crossroads
NAMES.i: Legba is the Fon trickster and divine linguist who stands between humans and the gods. Every ceremony begins by asking him to open the way, and in Haitian Vodou he lives on as Papa Legba.

NAMES.m: Beloved lwa of love, beauty, and tenderness
NAMES.i: Erzulie (Ezili) is the Haitian Vodou lwa of love, beauty, and devotion, whose name and character grew from West African water and love spirits. Her altars are dressed in perfume, pink and blue cloth, and fresh flowers.

NAMES.m: Iron-smith protector, defender of the people
NAMES.i: Ogou is the lwa of iron, forge-fire, and just leadership, honored in Vodou as a protector who fights for his community. He is the divine blacksmith whose tools clear paths and defend the vulnerable.

NAMES.m: Earth-lord of healing and fertile soil
NAMES.i: Sakpata is the Fon earth deity, honored as the master of soil, harvest, and the healing of the sick. His priests keep a sacred bond between the people and the ground beneath them.

NAMES.m: Rainbow serpent who carries the world
NAMES.i: Aido Hwedo is the cosmic rainbow serpent who carried Mawu through creation, and whose coils shaped hills and valleys. The rainbow in the sky is said to be his sign, and his weight is balanced by the world resting on his coils.

NAMES.m: Thunder-lord of storm, lightning, and justice
NAMES.i: Xevioso (Hevioso) is the Fon deity of thunder and lightning, who sends rain and cleansing storms. His thunderstones are treasured, and he is honored as an enforcer of truth and justice.
Agbe is the Ewe and Fon deity of the sea, ruler of the ocean's depths and the creatures within. Coastal communities honor him with offerings for safe fishing and calm waters.

NAMES.m: Ancient mother who birthed the divine twins
NAMES.i: In many Fon accounts Nana Buluku is the primordial creator who gave birth to Mawu and Lisa, then withdrew to let them make the world. She is the quiet source from which all other spirits arise.

NAMES.m: Forest spirit who gives gifts of wisdom
NAMES.i: The Aziza are small forest spirits in Fon tradition, helpers who teach hunters and healers the secrets of plants and animals. They are said to live in silk-cotton trees and share knowledge with the humble.

NAMES.m: Blessed son born after the twins
NAMES.i: Dossou is a traditional Fon and Ewe name given to a boy born after twins, a child who arrives in a household already marked by blessing. Twins are revered in the region, and the next child inherits the family's special grace.

NAMES.m: Blessed daughter born after the twins
NAMES.i: Dossi is the feminine counterpart of Dossou, given to a girl born after twins in Fon and Ewe families. It carries the sense of a gift arriving after double joy.

NAMES.m: Child of Wednesday, bright and spirited
NAMES.i: Kokou is a day-name given to a boy born on Wednesday among the Ewe and Fon of Togo and Benin. Day-names tie a child to the rhythm of the week and the character of that day.

NAMES.m: Sky-father, giver of light and rain
NAMES.i: Nyame is the Akan supreme being of the sky, associated with light, rain, and creation. Akan names like Nyamekye, 'gift of God', carry his name as a blessing on a child.

NAMES.m: Earth-mother of harvest and fertile fields
NAMES.i: Asase Yaa is the Akan goddess of the earth, born on Thursday, who nurtures crops and receives the dead. Farmers traditionally rest on her day to honor the soil.

NAMES.m: Calm daughter of Monday, born to peace
NAMES.i: Adwoa is the Akan day-name for a girl born on Monday, often linked to the word dwo, meaning calm or cool. It is given with the wish that the child be peaceful and gentle.

NAMES.m: Daughter of Sunday, bright with blessing
NAMES.i: Akosua is the Akan day-name for a girl born on Sunday. Her brother-name Kwasi (Kosi) completes the pair, and Sunday children are often seen as blessed.
Kofi is the Akan day-name for a boy born on Friday, famously borne by Kofi Annan. Friday-born children are traditionally thought to love adventure and journeys.

In the Kebra Nagast, Menelik is the son of Solomon and Queen Makeda. He travels to Jerusalem to meet his father and returns to Ethiopia with the Ark of the Covenant. He is remembered as the first king of the Solomonic dynasty.

Kokeb is the Ge'ez and Amharic word for star. Ethiopian Christian poetry often uses star imagery for guidance, as in the star that led travelers to a holy birth. It is a loved name for a daughter who is expected to guide others.

Tsehay means sun in Ge'ez and Amharic. It is a name of warmth and brightness, given to girls born at dawn or into a sunlit season. It was borne by Empress Tsehay, one of Ethiopia's best known royal women.

Genet is the Ge'ez and Amharic word for Eden or paradise, a walled garden of delight. It appears throughout Ethiopian Orthodox hymns and homilies. Parents choose it to wish a child a life as peaceful as paradise.
Mihret means mercy or compassion in Ge'ez and Amharic. It appears in Ethiopian prayers that ask for divine mercy. It is often given to a child seen as a gift of grace after a long wait.

NAMES.m: First month of the year, bright with new rain-washed flowers
NAMES.i: Meskerem is the first month of the Ethiopian calendar, beginning on the New Year, Enkutatash. It comes as the long rains end and the hills turn green and gold. The name suggests a fresh start.

NAMES.m: Zion, the holy mountain of promise
NAMES.i: Tsion is the Ge'ez form of Zion. In the Kebra Nagast, Ethiopia becomes the new Zion when the Ark of the Covenant comes to Aksum. The church of St. Mary of Zion in Aksum is said to keep the Ark, and the name is deeply loved.

NAMES.m: King whose sovereignty the bees recognize
NAMES.i: Lalibela was a Zagwe king who, according to tradition, had the rock-hewn churches of Lalibela carved from living stone. The name is said to mean that bees recognized his future sovereignty at his birth. The town that bears it is a sacred pilgrimage site.

Saint Yared of Aksum is traditionally credited with inventing Ethiopian liturgical chant and its musical notation in the 6th century. Tradition says he learned his melodies from the song of three birds. His name now stands for sacred music.

NAMES.m: King of Aksum, bringer of the new faith
NAMES.i: Ezana was the 4th-century king of Aksum who brought Christianity to the kingdom. His coins and stone inscriptions record his reign and his conversion. The name suggests a leader who guides a people toward light.

NAMES.m: My strength, steady as the mountains
NAMES.i: Haile means 'my strength' or 'my power' in Amharic. It often begins compound names such as Haile Selassie, 'Power of the Trinity,' and Haile Mariam. It carries the idea of strength given by God.

Berhane means light in Ge'ez and is a common name across Ethiopia and Eritrea. Ethiopian scripture and hymns use light as a symbol of truth and divine presence. It is given to boys and girls alike as a wish for a bright path.

Dawit is the Ethiopian form of David. In the Kebra Nagast Solomon's father David is the root of the royal line, and Ethiopian Christians treasure his Psalms. Many generations of Ethiopian children have learned to chant them.

Tewodros comes from the Greek Theodoros, 'gift of God.' An Ethiopian prophecy in the Kebra Nagast tradition foretells a just king named Tewodros who will restore the nation. Emperor Tewodros II took the name in the 19th century to claim that role.
Tsegaye is built from tsega, 'grace' or 'gift,' with the possessive ending -ye, 'my.' It means 'my grace,' a child seen as a blessing. It is common in Amharic-speaking families.

Amanuel is the Ethiopian form of Immanuel, from the Hebrew for 'God is with us.' It is widely used among Ethiopian and Eritrean Christians as a name of protection and faith. It is a gentle wish that a child will never walk alone.

NAMES.m: Diamond, a bright and enduring jewel
NAMES.i: Almaz means diamond in Amharic, a stone that stands for brilliance and endurance. It is a classic Ethiopian girls' name, used for generations as a sign of how precious a daughter is.

Ninigi-no-Mikoto is the grandson of Amaterasu. He descended from the High Plain of Heaven to rule the earthly land, carrying the sacred mirror, sword and jewel. His name evokes the bright ripeness of rice ears.

Toyotama-hime is the daughter of the sea god Watatsumi. She lived in a palace of fish-scale roofs beneath the waves and married the hunter prince Hoori. Her son became the grandfather of the first emperor, Jimmu.
Omoikane is the kami of wisdom and deliberation. He devised the plan that lured Amaterasu from her cave, and the gods turned to him in every council.

NAMES.m: Moon, silver lamp of the night
NAMES.i: Tsuki is the plain word for the moon. The Man'yoshu poets watched it rise over the mountains and set over the sea, and it stands for longing and quiet beauty.

The pine stays green through winter and is a symbol of longevity and constancy. It also puns on the verb matsu, 'to wait', and Man'yoshu poets knotted pine branches as prayers for the safe return of loved ones.

NAMES.m: Plum blossom, flower that braves the cold
NAMES.i: In the Man'yoshu the plum was the favorite flower of spring, celebrated in a famous set of poems from a plum-blossom banquet at Dazaifu. It blooms while snow still lies on the ground.

NAMES.m: Calm of the sea when the waves lie still
NAMES.i: Nagi names the hush when wind and waves fall quiet on the sea. The same root appears in the divine name Izanagi, and the word has long carried the sense of peace.

NAMES.m: Inviter, divine father of the islands
NAMES.i: Izanagi and Izanami stirred the sea with a jeweled spear, and the drops that fell became the first island. He later purified himself in a river, and from his washing the sun, moon and storm kami were born.

NAMES.m: Spring mist, soft veil over the hills
NAMES.i: Kasumi is the haze that drifts over mountains in spring. Man'yoshu poets used it to herald the new season, a gentle veil over blossoms and distant peaks.

NAMES.m: Mist rising softly over river and field
NAMES.i: Sagiri is an old poetic word for mist, used in Man'yoshu verse for vapor rising at dawn above rivers. It suggests longing, quiet and the blurred edge between earth and sky.

NAMES.m: Heron, white and patient by the water
NAMES.i: The heron stands motionless in shallow water, a white figure of grace and patience. It appears in classical Japanese poetry as a bird of marshes and rice fields.

NAMES.m: Fresh ears of rice, abundance of the land
NAMES.i: Toyoashihara no Mizuho no Kuni, 'land of fresh rice ears', is an ancient poetic name for Japan in the Kojiki. It speaks of fertility, harvest and prosperity.

NAMES.m: Great harmony, the old heart of Japan
NAMES.i: Yamato is the ancient name of the region where Japan's early court arose. The Kojiki and Man'yoshu praise it as a land of green hills and beloved homes, and its characters read 'great harmony'.

NAMES.m: Madder-red glow of the evening sky
NAMES.i: Akane is the red dye plant, and the word was once a poetic epithet for the sun, as in 'akane sasu'. Princess Nukata used it in her famous Man'yoshu love poem to Prince Ōama.
Ōtomo no Tabito was a Man'yoshu poet and governor of Dazaifu. He hosted the plum-blossom banquet there and wrote tender poems on wine, loss and the passing of time.

NAMES.m: Keeper of the house, gatherer of songs
NAMES.i: Ōtomo no Yakamochi is the poet most often credited as the final compiler of the Man'yoshu. He wrote more than four hundred poems of the seasons, of friendship and of longing.

NAMES.m: Jewel-vessel to which spirits draw near
NAMES.i: Tamayori-hime is the sea goddess who raised her nephew Hoori's son and later married him. She became the mother of Emperor Jimmu. Her name means a vessel where tama, the soul or spirit, gathers.

NAMES.m: Moonlit night, silver hush over the land
NAMES.i: Tsukiyo, or tsukuyo, is the moonlit night that Man'yoshu poets loved. Under it lovers walk, travelers remember home, and the whole world turns silver.

NAMES.m: Elegance, refinement of the courtly heart
NAMES.i: Miyabi is the courtly ideal of grace, refinement and delicate feeling, rooted in the Man'yoshu and Heian court. It was an aesthetic of poetry, music and the sensitive eye.
NAMES.src: Man'yoshu (c. 759 CE) and Heian court tradition

NAMES.m: Valiant heart, the bright hero of Yamato
NAMES.i: Yamato Takeru is the young prince of the Kojiki who journeyed across the land to unite its peoples. His story ends in longing for home, and he sings of Yamato as the loveliest land among its green mountains.

NAMES.m: Moon goddess of the silver palace
NAMES.i: Chang'e swallowed the elixir of immortality and floated up to the moon, where she lives in the Cold Palace with the Jade Rabbit. Every Mid-Autumn Festival, families gaze at the full moon and remember her.

NAMES.m: Faithful cowherd who loved a star
NAMES.i: The humble Cowherd found the weaver goddess bathing in a river and won her heart. Their love is celebrated every year at the Qixi Festival, when the two stars Altair and Vega draw near.
NAMES.src: Han dynasty folk tradition, Nineteen Old Poems (c. 2nd century CE)

NAMES.m: Free wandering of a carefree spirit
NAMES.i: 'Xiaoyao You', or 'Free and Easy Wandering', is the opening chapter of the Zhuangzi. It describes the Peng bird crossing the sky and a mind unbound by worldly measure.

NAMES.m: Great white star, bright as the evening planet
NAMES.i: Taibai is the courtesy name of the Tang poet Li Bai, and also the Chinese name of Venus. Legend says his mother dreamed of the Great White Star before his birth. He is said to have drowned reaching for the moon's reflection in a river.
NAMES.src: Tang dynasty poetry, Li Bai (701-762 CE)

NAMES.i: Zimei was the courtesy name of Du Fu, the 'Poet-Sage' of the Tang dynasty. His verses hold the common people's sorrows and a deep tenderness toward the world.
NAMES.src: Tang dynasty poetry, Du Fu (712-770 CE)

NAMES.m: Blue lotus rising pure from still water
NAMES.i: Li Bai styled himself 'Qinglian Jushi', the Blue Lotus Layman, after the lotus that grows unstained from mud. It is a lasting emblem of purity and unworldly grace.
NAMES.src: Tang dynasty poetry, Li Bai (8th century CE)

NAMES.m: Orchid pavilion of poets and flowing wine
NAMES.i: In 353 CE, Wang Xizhi gathered forty-one scholars at the Orchid Pavilion. They floated wine cups down a winding stream and composed poems, and he wrote his famous 'Preface' in calligraphy there. The preface is called the finest piece of running script ever written.

NAMES.m: One who is like water, gentle and enduring
NAMES.i: 'The highest good is like water' (上善若水) opens Chapter 8 of the Tao Te Ching. Water benefits all things without contending and settles in the places others disdain.
NAMES.src: Tao Te Ching, ch. 8 (c. 4th century BCE)

NAMES.m: Bright moon shining over distant homes
NAMES.i: Li Bai's 'Quiet Night Thought' opens with moonlight before his bed. The poem stirs longing for home, and the bright moon has since stood for reunion and remembrance.
The Book of Documents tells how, when the court music was played, the phoenix came and danced with dignity (鳳凰來儀). Its arrival is an omen of harmony and a wise reign.
NAMES.src: Shangshu (Book of Documents, c. 5th century BCE)

NAMES.m: Precious jade, a gift of lasting friendship
NAMES.i: In the Classic of Poetry, a gift of a quince is returned with 'qiongyao', beautiful jade, as a pledge of enduring friendship. The word came to mean the finest jade and the most treasured of gifts.

NAMES.m: Brocade zither whose strings sing of memory
NAMES.i: Li Shangyin's enigmatic 'Jinse' asks why the zither has fifty strings, each recalling the springtime of youth. Its image of Zhuangzi dreaming of a butterfly makes it one of the most beloved poems of the Tang.

NAMES.m: Jade pool of the Queen Mother of the West
NAMES.i: Yaochi is the lake of the Queen Mother of the West on Mount Kunlun, where the peaches of immortality ripen once in three thousand years. Poets have used it as a symbol of paradise.
NAMES.src: Mu Tianzi Zhuan and Shan Hai Jing (c. 4th century BCE)

NAMES.m: Azure cloud, high aspiration and lofty aims
NAMES.i: To 'step onto the azure clouds' (青雲直上) means to rise to high station and noble ideals. Tang poets used the cloud as a symbol of a lofty, unhurried spirit.
NAMES.src: Classical Chinese poetry, Tang dynasty tradition

NAMES.m: Southern mountain, a place of serene seclusion
NAMES.i: Tao Yuanming wrote, 'Picking chrysanthemums by the eastern fence, I see the southern mountain in the distance.' The line is a celebrated image of contentment in simple living.

NAMES.m: Deep clarity, a mind like still water
NAMES.i: Tao Yuanming left official life to farm, grow chrysanthemums, and write. He became China's great poet of rural retreat and wrote the Peach Blossom Spring, the tale of a hidden utopia.

NAMES.m: Moon's charioteer who gazes and unhurriedly soothes
NAMES.i: In the Chu Ci, Wangshu drives the moon's chariot across the heavens while Xihe drives the sun's. In poetry his name became a poetic word for the moon itself.

NAMES.m: Sun mother who guides the ten radiant suns
NAMES.i: Xihe is the mother of the ten suns, who bathes them in the Valley of Light and drives them across the sky in a dragon-drawn chariot. She is the origin of the calendar and the measuring of days.
NAMES.src: Shan Hai Jing (c. 4th century BCE-2nd century CE)

NAMES.m: Master of the zither and of true friendship
NAMES.i: Bo Ya's friend Zhong Ziqi could hear mountains and flowing rivers in his playing. When Ziqi died, Bo Ya broke his zither and never played again, since none was left who understood. The tale gave China the word 'zhiyin', soul-friend.

NAMES.m: Cold Mountain, a hermit-poet's lofty refuge
NAMES.i: Hanshan, the wandering Tang hermit-poet, wrote his verses on rocks and trees of Cold Mountain. His voice is playful, free, and quietly enlightened.
NAMES.src: Hanshan Shi (Tang dynasty, c. 8th-9th century CE)

NAMES.m: Bamboo grove of sages and music
NAMES.i: The Seven Sages of the Bamboo Grove were third-century poets and musicians, including Ruan Ji and Ji Kang. They met among the bamboo to drink, play the zither, and talk freely. Bamboo itself stands for resilience and integrity.

NAMES.m: Mysterious mother, the valley spirit that never dies
NAMES.i: Chapter 6 of the Tao Te Ching praises the 'Valley Spirit' as the 'Mysterious Female', the gateway from which heaven and earth arise. It is a source that is subtle and endless.
NAMES.src: Tao Te Ching, ch. 6 (c. 4th century BCE)

NAMES.m: Magnolia, a daughter of courage and filial devotion
NAMES.i: The Ballad of Mulan tells of a young woman who takes her father's place in the army and returns home to put on her old clothes and paint her face again. Her name means magnolia, a flower that blooms in early spring.
NAMES.src: Ballad of Mulan (Northern Wei, c. 5th-6th century CE)

NAMES.m: One who hears the cries of the world with compassion
NAMES.i: Guanyin, 'Perceiver of Sounds', is the bodhisattva of compassion, who hears every cry for help and answers it. She is often shown in white robes holding a vase of healing water and a willow branch.

NAMES.m: Dawn, the first pale light before the sun
NAMES.i: Saebyeok is the quiet hour just before sunrise, when Korean poetry often places farewells and new beginnings. Silla's founding legends open at dawn, when a strange light by the well Najeong announces a miraculous birth.
NAMES.src: Korean native vocabulary; Samguk Yusa (c. 1281) dawn imagery

NAMES.m: Pine tree, evergreen through every winter
NAMES.i: Sol is the native Korean word for pine, the tree of constancy that stays green under snow. It appears in the first line of the national anthem's 'Namsan pine,' and in countless sijo and hyangga-descended poems as a symbol of unbending integrity.
NAMES.src: Korean native vocabulary; Aegukga (national anthem) imagery

NAMES.m: Master archer, child of the sun and the river
NAMES.i: Jumong, born from an egg after his mother Yuhwa was touched by sunlight, was a peerless archer and became Dongmyeongseong, founder of Goguryeo. When pursued, he struck the river with his bow, and fish and turtles rose to form a bridge.

NAMES.m: Willow blossom, daughter of the river god
NAMES.i: Yuhwa (柳花) was the daughter of the river god Habaek and the mother of Jumong. Sunlight followed her into a chamber and she conceived a great egg, from which the founder of Goguryeo was born. She is remembered in Korean tradition as a protector of her son and a patron of grain.

NAMES.m: Lord of the river, keeper of deep waters
NAMES.i: Habaek (河伯), Count of the River, is the water deity in Goguryeo's founding myth and father of Yuhwa. In his river palace he tested the sky prince Haemosu in a contest of shape-shifting.

NAMES.m: Heavenly prince who brought light to the mountain
NAMES.i: Hwanung (桓雄), son of the Lord of Heaven Hwanin, longed to live among humans and descended to Mount Taebaek with three thousand followers. He brought wind, rain and cloud ministers, and taught people law, medicine and agriculture.

NAMES.m: Yam-boy who won a princess with a song
NAMES.i: Seodong (薯童), 'yam boy,' is the hyangga author said to have taught children a rhyme about Princess Seonhwa so that she would be sent to him. He later became King Mu of Baekje, and the poem Seodong-yo is among the oldest Korean verse.

NAMES.m: Virtuous flower, a princess who followed her heart
NAMES.i: Princess Seonhwa (善花) of Silla, the third daughter of King Jinpyeong, is the heroine of the Seodong-yo story. Banished by the court, she travelled to Baekje and married the man who had sung of her, later becoming queen.

NAMES.m: Gracious dancer who answered betrayal with peace
NAMES.i: Cheoyong (處容) came home to find a plague spirit with his wife. Rather than rage, he sang and danced the hyangga Cheoyongga, and the spirit, moved by his generosity, vowed never to enter a home bearing his image. His mask became a protective charm.

NAMES.m: Bright moon, a monk who sang the heavens still
NAMES.i: Wolmyeong (月明) was a Silla monk-poet who wrote the hyangga Jemaemaga for his dead sister. When two suns appeared in the sky, his hymn Dosolga dispelled the omen, and legend says the moon paused its course to listen to his flute.

NAMES.m: Virtuous grace, a queen of keen foresight
NAMES.i: Queen Seondeok (善德, r. 632-647) was Silla's first reigning queen. Tradition says she foresaw an invasion from the sound of frogs and the scent of peonies, and she built Cheomseongdae, the oldest surviving observatory in East Asia.

NAMES.m: Radiance that illumines the whole world
NAMES.i: Hyeokgeose (赫居世), 'bright ruler of the world,' hatched from a gleaming egg beside the well Najeong, where a white horse knelt in reverence. At thirteen he was made king and founded Silla in 57 BCE, and his body was said to radiate light.

NAMES.m: Dragon-born queen of the sacred well
NAMES.i: Alyeong (閼英) was born from the side of a dragon at the well Aryeong, with a face of great beauty but a beak-like mouth that fell away after bathing in a stream. She became the queen of Hyeokgeose and ruled beside him as one of the 'Two Sages.'

NAMES.m: Founding queen who crossed the sea to build a kingdom
NAMES.i: Soseono (召西奴) was a merchant's daughter, wife of Jumong, and the mother of Biryu and Onjo. After Jumong's heir arrived she led her sons south and helped found Baekje, becoming one of Korea's most remembered women founders.

NAMES.m: Flowing stream, a prince of rushing waters
NAMES.i: Biryu (沸流), elder son of Soseono, took his people to the coast at Michuhol in the Baekje founding tradition. His name evokes the Biryu river and the Biryu-guk polity of Goguryeo's early lands.

NAMES.m: Golden jade, a princess who crossed the sea
NAMES.i: Heo Hwangok (許黃玉), a princess of Ayuta, was told in a dream by the Lord of Heaven to sail to Korea and marry King Suro. She crossed the sea in a ship with a red sail and became queen of Geumgwan Gaya, and she is the ancestor of the Gimhae Heo clan.

NAMES.m: First to appear, a king born of golden light
NAMES.i: Suro (首露), 'the first to appear,' came down from heaven as one of six golden eggs in a purple cord. The villagers sang the Gujiga, the hymn that summoned him, and he became the founder of Geumgwan Gaya in 42 CE.

NAMES.m: Blue-grey one, tinted like the steppe sky
NAMES.i: Börte Üjin was the first wife of Temüjin, later Chinggis Khan. When the Merkits abducted her, he rode to rescue her. The name comes from the word for the grey-blue color of the wolf and the endless sky.

NAMES.m: Smith of iron, forger of strength
NAMES.i: This was the birth name of Chinggis Khan. The Secret History says his father Yesügei named him after a Tatar chief he had just defeated. The name comes from temür, 'iron', and means one who forges it.

NAMES.m: Wise sage, counselor of the people
NAMES.i: Bilge Khagan ruled the Second Turkic Khaganate and is named on the Orkhon stelae. His inscription urges his people to remember their roots and stay united beneath the eternal blue sky. The word means 'wise' in both Turkic and Mongolic traditions.

Kül Tegin was the brother of Bilge Khagan and a brilliant commander. His memorial stele, raised in 732 CE in the Orkhon Valley, is one of the oldest known Turkic texts. The name joins kül, 'fame' or 'glory', with tegin, 'prince'.
NAMES.src: Orkhon inscriptions, Kül Tegin stele (732 CE)

NAMES.m: Eternal blue sky, the heaven above all
NAMES.i: Tengri, or Tenger, is the sky god at the center of steppe belief. The Orkhon inscriptions open with 'When the blue sky above and the dark earth below were created, between them human beings were created.' In Mongolian the word still means both 'sky' and 'heaven'.

NAMES.m: Golden eagle, lord of the high sky
NAMES.i: The golden eagle is the great hunting bird of the steppe, trained by Mongol and Kazakh falconers for centuries. It stands for courage, freedom, and keen sight. The word is still a favored name for boys.
NAMES.src: Mongolian steppe tradition; Secret History of the Mongols

NAMES.i: In the Secret History, Dobun Mergen's ancestors dream of a white falcon carrying the sun and moon. It lands on the hand of Yesügei, Chinggis Khan's father, and foretells a great son. The falcon became a sign of royal destiny among the Mongols.

NAMES.m: Sun, golden light of the steppe morning
NAMES.i: Naran means 'sun' in Mongolian, as in Naran Tuul, 'sun market'. Together with the moon it is a sacred emblem on the Mongolian Soyombo symbol. A child with this name is wished a bright and warming life.

NAMES.m: Wild rose, bloom of the steppe
NAMES.i: Sarnai is the Mongolian wild rose that blooms in the valleys and on the steppe edges in summer. It is a popular girl's name, a symbol of gentle beauty with thorns that protect it. The name suggests a delicate but resilient spirit.
From ariun, 'pure, clean, holy', a word used for clear water and sacred places across the steppe. The Mongols value purity of heart, and this name wishes the girl a life of clarity and goodness.

NAMES.m: Ray of light, first beam of dawn
NAMES.i: Tuyaa means a ray or beam of light, like the first sunlight on the horizon of the grasslands. The name carries the image of the sun rising over the steppe. It is a common and beloved name for girls in modern Mongolia.

NAMES.m: Morning star, bright herald of the dawn
NAMES.i: Tsolmon is the Mongolian name for Venus, the bright star that shines before sunrise. Herders watch it to know when dawn is near. The name suggests a bright promise at the edge of night.

NAMES.m: River of silver waters, flowing and life-giving
NAMES.i: The Selenge is Mongolia's greatest river. It flows north into Lake Baikal and nourishes the pastures along its course. The name is used for girls and also for a province.
NAMES.src: Mongolian geographic tradition; Secret History of the Mongols

NAMES.m: Rising one, flourishing like the new dawn
NAMES.i: Mandukhai Khatun, 'the Wise', was a 15th-century queen who reunited the Mongols after years of division. She led armies in battle while pregnant and raised the young Dayan Khan to the throne. Her name comes from mandu-, 'to rise or flourish'.

NAMES.m: River of the sacred valley, keeper of ancestors
NAMES.i: The Orkhon River runs through the valley where the Turkic khagans raised their stone memorials. These carved the earliest known Turkic writing, and the valley was a center of steppe power for centuries. The name carries the sense of heritage, memory, and flowing water.

NAMES.m: Goddess of lightning who guards the sea with a crystal orb
NAMES.i: In the Ramakien, Mekhala is the sea-guardian goddess who rescues sailors. She flashes her crystal ball to dazzle the giant Ramasura, who chases her with a thunder-axe. Thai tradition explains lightning and thunder this way.

NAMES.m: Golden day, a woman of luminous beauty
NAMES.i: Wanthong is the central heroine of Khun Chang Khun Phaen, loved by two men and caught between their rivalry. Her name joins wan (day) and thong (gold), and she remains one of the most discussed women in Thai literature.
NAMES.src: Khun Chang Khun Phaen (Ayutthaya-era oral epic, written down 19th c.)

NAMES.i: Busaba is the princess beloved by Prince Inao in the Thai Inao epic, a tale of the Javanese Panji cycle adapted for the Siamese court. Her name comes from Sanskrit pushpa, 'flower', and has been a refined classical choice for girls for generations.
NAMES.src: Inao (Thai court epic, Rama II era)

NAMES.i: In the Ramakien, Sida is the wife of Phra Ram, born from the earth and abducted by the demon king Thotsakan. Her faith and endurance through captivity and trial make her the model of devotion in Thai tradition.

NAMES.s: พิมพิลาไลย
NAMES.m: Graceful beauty, lovely as a carved image
NAMES.i: Phim Philalai is Khun Phaen's first wife and the young woman Wanthong's story turns on. She is a graceful figure of Ayutthaya's folk epic. Her name pairs phim (image, form) with an ornate Pali-Sanskrit term for elegance.

Benchakai is the daughter of the wise Phiphek in the Ramakien. She is sent in the guise of Sida to deceive Phra Ram, an episode known for her loyalty and beauty. Her name suggests five bodies or forms.

NAMES.m: Vast sky, open and cloudless heaven
NAMES.i: Napha is a Sanskrit-derived Thai word for the open sky, used often in royal-register poetry for the heavens that cradle sun, moon and stars. As a given name it suggests a spacious, serene spirit.

NAMES.m: Dawn, the rosy light before sunrise
NAMES.i: Arunee is the feminine form of Aruna, the dawn charioteer of the sun in Indic myth. It is honored in Thailand through Wat Arun, the Temple of Dawn. The name evokes the first gold-pink glow on the river.
Kusuma is the Pali-Sanskrit word for flower, and it appears in classical Thai verse and in temple naming. It is a quiet, elegant name for girls of Buddhist families.

Phra Aphaimani is the flute-playing prince of Sunthorn Phu's great verse romance. His music can put giants to sleep and charm sea ogresses. His name joins apphai (freedom from fear, forgiveness) with mani (jewel).
NAMES.src: Phra Aphai Mani by Sunthorn Phu (early 19th c.)

NAMES.i: Phiphek is the Ramakien's Vibhishana, the younger brother of the demon king Thotsakan. He speaks truth to power, leaves Lanka for Phra Ram's side, and is crowned its ruler after the war. He stands for conscience and wise counsel.

NAMES.m: Pleasing one, a gentle and righteous prince
NAMES.i: Phra Ram is the hero of the Ramakien, an avatar of Vishnu and the model of the just king. Thai kings of the Chakri dynasty take the title Rama, and the name carries a sense of virtue and calm.

In the Ramakien, the white monkey Hanuman is Phra Ram's most faithful general, famed for his shape-shifting and his leap across the sea to Lanka. Thai tradition adds playful and clever touches to his character, and he stands for loyalty and boundless strength.

NAMES.m: Beloved prince, graceful lover and wanderer
NAMES.i: Inao is the romantic hero of the Thai court epic adapted from the Javanese Panji tales. He is a prince who roams through forests and kingdoms, searching for Busaba, his love. He is a classic figure of Thai dance-drama.
NAMES.src: Inao (Thai court epic, Rama II era)

NAMES.i: Rawee is a Sanskrit-derived Thai word for the sun, used in poetry alongside Aphisit and Athit. It remains a popular modern name for boys, suggesting warmth and clarity.

NAMES.m: Jewel-like young hero of noble courage
NAMES.i: Phlai Kaew is the childhood name of Khun Phaen, hero of the Khun Chang Khun Phaen epic. He grows into a famed warrior, lover and master of spells. Kaew means 'crystal' or 'gem', a classical image of preciousness.

NAMES.m: Radiant young envoy of courage and honor
NAMES.i: Ongkot is the Ramakien's monkey prince Angada, son of Phali, who serves Phra Ram as a bold ambassador. He goes to the court of Thotsakan and stands firm there. Thai performance traditions celebrate his steady heart.

NAMES.m: Noble monkey king of faithful alliance
NAMES.i: Sukhrip is the Ramakien's monkey king Sugriva, restored to his throne with Phra Ram's help. He then leads his armies to rescue Sida. His story is about gratitude, kept promises and friendship.

Thúy Kiều is the heroine of Nguyễn Du's epic, a gifted poet and musician whose beauty and devotion carry her through fifteen years of wandering. Her name has become a byword for Vietnamese womanhood and resilience.

NAMES.m: Kingfisher-green jade, a shimmering emerald hue
NAMES.i: The poem opens with the Vương sisters, Thúy Kiều and Thúy Vân, 'two peerless beauties' in the first lines. Thúy recalls the iridescent green of the kingfisher's feathers and of fine jade.

NAMES.m: Cloud, a soft drifting veil across the sky
NAMES.i: Thúy Vân is Kiều's younger sister, praised for a face as full as the moon and a calm, untroubled fortune. She marries Kim Trọng in the end and keeps the family's love whole.

NAMES.m: Moon, the silver lantern of the night
NAMES.i: The moon is Nguyễn Du's recurring witness. Kiều and Kim Trọng exchange vows beneath its light, and it later looks down on her loneliness. Nguyệt is the classical Sino-Vietnamese word for the moon.

NAMES.m: Fragrance, the sweet breath of blossoms
NAMES.i: Incense and flower scent drift through Nguyễn Du's verses, in garden meetings and in rites for ancestors. Hương is a beloved name for a girl said to carry grace like perfume.

NAMES.m: Willow, slender and swaying in the spring wind
NAMES.i: The willow is a classic image of feminine grace in Vietnamese poetry, and Nguyễn Du uses it for slender figures and for farewells by the riverbank. Its drooping branches suggest gentleness that bends and does not break.

NAMES.m: Silk, smooth, lustrous and finely woven
NAMES.i: Vietnamese silk from villages like Hà Đông is a symbol of refinement, and the poem's verses often liken soft skin and clothing to silk. Lụa is an uncommon given name, tender and evocative.

NAMES.m: Serene immortal, a quiet fairy of verse
NAMES.i: Đạm Tiên is the celebrated singer-poet whose tomb Kiều encounters at Thanh Minh. Moved to compose a lament for her, Kiều is later visited by her spirit in a dream, which gives the poem its sense of fate.
Sư Giác Duyên is the compassionate Buddhist nun who shelters Kiều at Quan Âm temple and guides her to safety. Her name joins awakening with the bonds of karma that draw people together.

NAMES.m: Golden esteem, a treasured and honorable man
NAMES.i: Kim Trọng is the scholar Kiều loves at first sight in the spring garden. His faithfulness after years of separation completes the poem's arc of constancy.

NAMES.m: Calm ocean, a free and boundless sea
NAMES.i: Từ Hải is the heroic outlaw who recognizes Kiều's worth and frees her from the brothel. He is portrayed as a man as free and wide as the sea, whose name Hải means ocean.

NAMES.m: Noble vision, a scholar of clear sight
NAMES.i: Vương Quan is Kiều's devoted younger brother, a scholar who searches for his lost sister and helps bring the family together again. His name suggests honor and clear sight.

NAMES.m: Jade, a precious and luminous gemstone
NAMES.i: Jade stands for purity, beauty and moral worth throughout Vietnamese and East Asian culture, and Nguyễn Du often compares his heroines to it. Ngọc is given to daughters and sons alike.

In the Javanese Ramayana, Sinta is the radiant wife of Rama, found in a plowed furrow of the earth. In wayang performances her loyalty through exile and captivity makes her the ideal of grace under trial.

NAMES.m: Bright, silver-white archer of clear purpose
NAMES.i: Arjuna is the beloved third Pandawa of the Javanese wayang, a graceful, refined hero and meditating ascetic. The Kakawin Arjunawiwaha tells how his austerities on Mount Indrakila won him divine weapons and a place among the gods.
Candra, the moon, glows through Javanese poetry as a symbol of serene beauty. Court poets used the word in verses and in 'candrasengkala', chronograms that encode dates in poetic imagery.

NAMES.m: Sun of golden dawn and daily blessing
NAMES.i: Surya is the sun god of the Hindu epics, remembered in Java through Kakawin tradition and Balinese-Javanese ritual. Surya is also the father of Karna in the Mahabharata, a hero of great generosity.
NAMES.src: Old Javanese Mahabharata adaptations (Adiparwa, c. 996 CE)

NAMES.m: Wind of vital breath and gentle strength
NAMES.i: Bayu, from Sanskrit Vayu, is the wind god and the divine father of Bima in the wayang Mahabharata. In Javanese the word names both the breeze and the breath that sustains life.
NAMES.src: Javanese wayang purwa tradition; Old Javanese Mahabharata

NAMES.i: Banyu is the everyday Javanese word for water, found in old songs and in place names such as Banyuwangi, 'fragrant water'. In Javanese thought water stands for purity, humility, and the ability to adapt.
Kencana, from Sanskrit kancana, means gold and appears in Malay and Javanese court verse for royal splendor. In classical Malay tales a golden-hued princess is often called Puteri Kencana.

NAMES.m: Harmony, the sweet tuning of music
NAMES.i: In Javanese gamelan, 'laras' is the tuning system, as in slendro and pelog. To name a child Laras is to wish a life in harmony, like instruments sounding together.

NAMES.m: Blossom, fragrant flower of noble birth
NAMES.i: Kusuma, 'flower' in Sanskrit and Old Javanese, was a favorite in royal names such as Kusumawardhani. Poets praised 'kusuma' as the image of beauty that opens in due season.

NAMES.m: Delightful hero of virtue and calm
NAMES.i: Rama is the ideal prince of the Ramayana, retold in the Javanese Kakawin Ramayana and carved on the Prambanan temple reliefs. His name means 'pleasing', and his steady virtue is a model for kingship.

NAMES.m: Gentle mother of the mighty Hanuman
NAMES.i: In the Javanese Ramayana, Anjani is the celestial nymph whose devotion brings forth Hanuman, the white monkey hero. Wayang tales cherish her as a symbol of loving motherhood and patient faith.
NAMES.src: Serat Rama; Javanese wayang purwa tradition

NAMES.i: Laksmana follows his brother Rama into forest exile and guards Sinta with unwavering devotion. In Javanese wayang he stands for brotherly loyalty and quiet courage.

NAMES.m: Sacred water of blessing and renewal
NAMES.i: Tirta, from Sanskrit tirtha, is holy water used in Javanese and Balinese rites of blessing. In the wayang Mahabharata, 'Tirta Amerta' is the elixir of immortality sought by gods and heroes.
NAMES.src: Old Javanese Adiparwa (c. 996 CE); Javanese ritual tradition

NAMES.m: Radiant sun lord and protector of people
NAMES.i: In Tagalog and Pampangan tradition, Apolaki is the god of the sun and a son of Bathala. His glow rules the day, and he guards warriors and the people with golden fire. In some tellings he shares the sky with his sister Mayari, the moon.

NAMES.m: Benevolent giver of the good harvest
NAMES.i: Dumangan is a Visayan god of the good harvest in Panay tradition. He blesses the fields with abundant crops and is remembered as a kindly provider who watches over the farmer's labor.

NAMES.m: Noble lord and chief of the people
NAMES.i: Lakan was a pre-colonial Tagalog title for a paramount chief, borne by rulers such as Lakandula of Tondo. As a given name it carries the sense of dignified, wise leadership.
NAMES.src: Pre-colonial Tagalog chiefly titles; Spanish chronicles (16th c.)

NAMES.m: Supreme creator, lord of sky and earth
NAMES.i: Bathala is the supreme creator god of the pre-colonial Tagalogs, who made the heavens, the earth, and the first people. The name is likely related to the Sanskrit-derived title bhattāraka, 'noble lord'. It evokes an all-embracing sky above the islands.
NAMES.src: Tagalog oral tradition; Plasencia's Customs of the Tagalogs (1589)

NAMES.m: Creator who dwells in the heights of heaven
NAMES.i: Kabunian is the supreme deity of the Ibaloi and Kankanaey peoples of the Cordillera. He lives in the sky above the mountains and gives life, rain, and the harvest. The name is spoken with reverence across the northern highlands.

NAMES.m: Radiant moon goddess of the night
NAMES.i: Mayari is the Tagalog goddess of the moon and a daughter of Bathala. In a famous tale she lost an eye in a duel with her brother Apolaki, and the moon now shines more softly than the sun. She is remembered as the lady who brings quiet light to the dark.

NAMES.m: Goddess of the morning and its first light
NAMES.i: Hanan is the Tagalog goddess of the morning, a daughter of Bathala in some traditions. She opens the day with gentle light before her brother Apolaki's full sun rises.

NAMES.m: Unwedded sky goddess, mother of the heavens
NAMES.i: In the Panay epic tradition, Alunsina is the primordial goddess of the highest heaven. She left her husband Datu Paubari and went to live in the upper sky, and the legends tell of her beauty, independence, and quiet grandeur.

NAMES.m: Dawn, the first light breaking over the sea
NAMES.i: Liwayway is the Tagalog word for dawn, the moment when the sky turns gold over the islands. It has long been used as a given name for girls, and it suggests new beginnings and hope.

NAMES.m: Gentle northeast breeze and bird of creation
NAMES.i: Amihan is the cool northeast monsoon wind of the Philippines. In a Tagalog creation tale she is a bird who pecked open a bamboo to free Malakas and Maganda, the first man and woman.

NAMES.m: Mother of the sea and keeper of its waves
NAMES.i: Aman Sinaya is the Tagalog goddess of the ocean. She was made by Bathala to rule the waters, and fishermen once called upon her for safe seas and good catches.

NAMES.m: Gentle mountain guardian of the forest
NAMES.i: Mariang Makiling is the beautiful spirit of Mount Makiling in Laguna, a guardian of the forest. In the tales she helps the poor and kind with gifts of gold and food, and she withdraws from those who are greedy.

NAMES.m: Maiden of blood, mother of the Hero Twins
NAMES.i: Xkik' (Xquic) was the daughter of an underworld lord. A skull's spittle touched her palm and she conceived Hunahpu and Xbalanque. She carried the light of the world's renewal.

NAMES.m: Grandmother creator, keeper of the days
NAMES.i: Ixmukane is the elder grandmother and day-keeper of the Popol Vuh. She helped shape the first people from ground white and yellow maize, and she cared for her grandsons the Hero Twins.

NAMES.m: Feathered serpent, wise maker among the waters
NAMES.i: In the Popol Vuh's creation, Q'uq'umatz lay in the primordial waters wrapped in blue-green feathers. He spoke with Heart of Sky and together they brought the world into being.

NAMES.m: Sovereign, ruler who speaks the world into being
NAMES.i: Tepew is the 'Sovereign' who joined Q'uq'umatz in the dark waters before creation. Their council of words raised mountains and valleys from the sea.

NAMES.m: Feathered serpent, bringer of wind and rain
NAMES.i: Kukulkan is the Yucatec feathered serpent, honored at Chichén Itzá. At each equinox the shadow of a serpent seems to descend the pyramid's stairs.
NAMES.src: Yucatec Maya tradition; Chichén Itzá inscriptions

NAMES.m: Lord of the heavens, patron of scribes and healers
NAMES.i: Itzamna is the old creator god of the Yucatec Maya, credited with giving people writing, calendars and medicine. He is shown as a wise elder who sits between earth and sky.

NAMES.m: Plumeria blossom, fragrant flower of spring
NAMES.i: Nikte' is the Yucatec word for the plumeria flower. The blossom was woven into offerings and gardens and became a name for girls across the Maya world.

NAMES.m: White flower, pure blossom of the dawn
NAMES.i: Sak Nikte' is the 'white flower' of Yucatec legend, a princess whose love story is still told in the Yucatán. Sak means white, bright or pure.

NAMES.m: Rain lord, giver of thunder and harvest
NAMES.i: Chaak is the Maya god of rain and lightning. He swings a lightning axe to crack the clouds, and farmers still call on him for water for their maize.

NAMES.m: Dew of the sky, gentle morning moisture
NAMES.i: Itzel is a well-loved Yucatec Maya name, linked with itz, the dew or sacred moisture that falls at dawn. It also connects to Itzamna and the Itzá people.

NAMES.m: Lord of the forest, guardian of wild lands and maize
NAMES.i: Yum Kaax is the Yucatec Maya lord of the wilds and of the maize field. Hunters and farmers asked his permission before taking from the forest.

NAMES.m: Ripening seed, yellow maize of new life
NAMES.i: Q'anil is a K'iche' day sign of the 260-day calendar, linked to seed, fertility and the ripening of maize. Daykeepers see it as a day of abundance.

NAMES.m: Thread of time, patron of weavers and artists
NAMES.i: B'atz' is the K'iche' day sign for thread and the weaving of time. In the Popol Vuh, Hun Batz' and Hun Chuen are the elder brothers of the Hero Twins and patrons of music, writing and the arts.

NAMES.m: Wind, breath of life and spirit
NAMES.i: Ik' is the Maya word and day sign for wind, breath and life. A glyph shaped like a T stands for it in Classic inscriptions.
NAMES.src: Maya calendar tradition; Classic Maya glyphs

NAMES.m: Radiant sun-faced lord, bright as noon
NAMES.i: K'inich means 'sun-eyed' or 'radiant'. It is the title of the Maya sun god and of great Classic kings such as K'inich Janaab' Pakal of Palenque.

NAMES.m: New sun, green season of renewal
NAMES.i: Yaxk'in is a month of the Haab' calendar, the 'new' or 'green' sun that follows the rains. It marks a season of fresh light and growth.

NAMES.m: Lady painter, goddess of weaving and the arts
NAMES.i: Ixchebel Yax is a Maya goddess of weaving, painting and the arts, recorded among the Yucatec deities in Landa's account. She is seen as a daughter or companion of Ixchel.

NAMES.m: Flower, bloom of the earth's heart
NAMES.i: Xochitl is the Nahuatl word for flower, and it is also the 14th day-sign's cousin in poetry, where 'in xochitl in cuicatl' (flower and song) means art and truth itself. Flowers were seen as a gift from the gods and a symbol of beauty that passes quickly.

NAMES.m: Precious feather, plume of the quetzal bird
NAMES.i: Quetzalli names the long iridescent green tail feathers of the resplendent quetzal. Only nobles and priests could wear them, and the Mexica valued them above gold as a symbol of something precious and sacred.

NAMES.m: Maguey goddess, nourisher of a thousand drops
