NAMES.i: Mayahuel was the goddess of the maguey plant, whose sap became aguamiel, a sweet drink, and then pulque. Myth gives her four hundred breasts to feed her divine children, the Centzon Totochtin, the rabbits of drunkenness.

NAMES.m: She of the jade skirt, lady of flowing waters
NAMES.i: Chalchiuhtlicue was goddess of rivers, lakes, and the sea, and ruler of the Fourth Sun. Wearing a skirt of jade, the color of precious water, she was the patron of newborns, who were bathed in her name.
NAMES.src: Legend of the Suns (1558); Florentine Codex, Book 1

NAMES.i: Yoloxochitl combines yollotl (heart) and xochitl (flower). It is the name of the magnolia, a flower with a heart-shaped bud that the Mexica used as a remedy for the heart and a fragrant offering.

NAMES.m: Spring, fountain welling up from the earth
NAMES.i: Ameyalli means a spring of fresh water, the place where the earth gives water without being asked. In a valley of lakes and sacred springs, it evokes clarity and gentle abundance.

NAMES.m: Feathered serpent, bringer of wisdom and wind
NAMES.i: Quetzalcoatl was the feathered serpent god of wind, learning, and the dawn star, and he was said to have given maize and the calendar to humankind. He was a priest-king of Tula who sailed away east, promising to return.
NAMES.src: Legend of the Suns (1558); Florentine Codex, Book 3

NAMES.i: Tlaloc was the god of rain, lightning, and fertile fields, and he lived in the mountains, where he kept the clouds. The great double temple of Tenochtitlan was dedicated to him and to Huitzilopochtli, and the Mexica honored him for the maize his rains brought.

Nezahualcoyotl (1402–1472) was the poet-king of Texcoco, famed for his songs on the fleeting beauty of life and for his engineering and laws. His poems ask whether anything on earth lasts, and he built gardens of flowers and song.

NAMES.m: Wind, the breath that moves the world
NAMES.i: Ehecatl is the wind and the aspect of Quetzalcoatl who sweeps the way for the rain gods. In myth he breathed life into the bones of earlier humanity, and the day-sign Ehecatl, wind, is the second of the twenty.

NAMES.m: Descending eagle, falling like the setting sun
NAMES.i: Cuauhtemoc was the last Mexica tlatoani, who defended Tenochtitlan in 1521 against the Spanish and became a symbol of courage and dignity. His name refers to the sun as an eagle descending at dusk, which he would also later rise.
NAMES.src: Florentine Codex, Book 12; Anales de Tlatelolco

NAMES.m: Flower prince, lord of song, dance, and joy
NAMES.i: Xochipilli was the god of flowers, summer, games, music, and poetry. A famed stone statue shows him seated and covered with carved blossoms, in a state of ecstatic vision.

NAMES.m: Maize god, the divine ear of corn
NAMES.i: Centeotl was the god of maize, the sacred crop that the Mexica believed had formed the human body. Born from the earth goddess Tlazolteotl, he is shown in codices with the golden hair of the ripening ear.

Itztli is obsidian, the volcanic glass that the Mexica shaped into mirrors, blades, and jewelry. Its polished surface was a mirror of the soul, and it was linked with Tezcatlipoca, the Smoking Mirror.

NAMES.m: Cloud, soft herald of the rain
NAMES.i: Mixtli is the Nahuatl word for cloud. Clouds gathered around the mountain homes of Tlaloc and carried the water for the maize, and their drifting forms were read for omens.

NAMES.m: Movement, the earth's dance and the sun's turning
NAMES.i: Ollin means movement and is one of the twenty day-signs of the Mexica calendar. It is also the name of the Fifth Sun, the age of movement, and the Mexica believed the world was kept alive by the motion of the sun and the earth.
NAMES.src: Legend of the Suns (1558); Aztec Sun Stone

NAMES.m: Lightning bringer of rain across the highlands
NAMES.i: Illapa was the Andean god of thunder, lightning and rain. He was imagined as a man in shining clothes who struck stones from a sling to send rain pouring from the Milky Way, the celestial river.
NAMES.src: Inca oral tradition; chronicles of Cristóbal de Molina (c. 1575)

NAMES.m: Condor, soaring lord of the high mountain sky
NAMES.i: The Andean condor was sacred to the Quechua as a messenger between earth and the upper world of Hanan Pacha. It is still honored as a spirit of the mountain, the apus, and is a symbol of freedom.

Tupaq, often spelled Túpac, was a royal Inca name borne by Tupaq Inca Yupanqui, who expanded the empire to Chile and Ecuador. It evokes brilliance and noble splendor, and it was carried forward by Tupac Amaru II in his 1780 uprising.
NAMES.src: Garcilaso de la Vega, Comentarios Reales (1609)

NAMES.m: Transformer of the world, bringer of new epochs
NAMES.i: Pachakuti Inca Yupanqui, the ninth Sapa Inca, turned a small kingdom into Tawantinsuyu and is credited with building Machu Picchu. His name means the turning over of time and space, a world made anew.
NAMES.src: Garcilaso de la Vega, Comentarios Reales (1609)

NAMES.m: Hero of the high terraces, a lover who defied a king
NAMES.i: Ollantay is the hero of a classic Quechua drama in which a general loves Princess Cusi Coyllur and defies the Inca Pachakuti. The place Ollantaytambo, with its great stone terraces, bears his name.

NAMES.m: Mountain lord, guardian spirit of the peaks
NAMES.i: In Andean belief every great snow peak is an apu, a living protector of the valleys below. Villagers still leave coca leaves and chicha as offerings to ask the mountain for safe passage and good harvests.

NAMES.m: Stone, steadfast and enduring as the Andes
NAMES.i: Rumi is the Quechua word for stone, the material of Inca masonry whose fitted walls have outlasted earthquakes for centuries. As a name it suggests quiet resilience.

NAMES.m: Splendid founder, first lord of the Inca
NAMES.i: In the founding legend, Manco Capac rose with his sister-wife Mama Ocllo from Lake Titicaca, sent by Inti with a golden staff. Where the staff sank into the earth at Cusco, he built the Inca capital.
NAMES.src: Garcilaso de la Vega, Comentarios Reales (1609)

NAMES.m: Dawn star, bright Venus with flowing hair
NAMES.i: Chaska is the Quechua name for Venus as morning and evening star. The word also describes a star with long, rayed locks, and Inca poetry uses it for a beautiful maiden with flowing hair.
Quri, spelled Qori or Cori in older sources, is gold, the sweat of the sun in Inca belief. It appears in Qorikancha, the 'golden enclosure' temple in Cusco, and in names such as Cori Coillur.
Sumaq means beautiful or exquisite in Quechua. It lives in the stage name of the Peruvian singer Yma Sumac, 'how beautiful,' and in the Quechua greeting of admiration for a lovely land.

NAMES.m: Dawn light, the first gleam over the mountains
NAMES.i: Illari is the first glimmer of sunrise as it touches the snow peaks. It comes from the Quechua root for shining, and it suits a child who arrives at dawn.

NAMES.m: Star, a small light in the Andean night
NAMES.i: Kuyllur, also written Qoyllur, is the Quechua word for star. The Inca watched the stars closely, and the pilgrimage of Qoyllur Rit'i, 'snow star,' still climbs to a glacier each year beneath the Pleiades.

NAMES.m: Queen, noble consort of the Sapa Inca
NAMES.i: Quya, written Coya in Spanish chronicles, was the title of the Inca queen and chief wife of the Sapa Inca. She had her own ceremonial duties and was linked with Mama Killa, the moon.
NAMES.src: Garcilaso de la Vega, Comentarios Reales (1609)

NAMES.m: Love, tender will and heartfelt care
NAMES.i: Munay is the Quechua word for love and loving will. Along with yachay (knowledge) and ruway (action), it is one of the three principles of Andean life.
Built from ara (day, sky, time) and sy (mother), the name evokes the dawn that gives birth to each new day. It is used across Paraguay and Brazil, sometimes spelled Araçy.

NAMES.m: Flower, blossom opening in the forest
NAMES.i: Yvoty is the everyday Guaraní word for flower. It is a tender name for a girl, echoing the blossoms of the Paraguayan lapacho and the orchids of the Atlantic forest.

NAMES.m: Lady of the waters, singer of the river
NAMES.i: From y (water) and ara (lady), Iara is the river-lady of Tupi-Guaraní lore, whose song draws listeners to the water's edge. Today the name is popular in Brazil and the Guaraní-speaking south, honoring the beauty and mystery of rivers.

NAMES.m: Sacred word, the voice that carries the soul
NAMES.i: Ayvu means voice or language, and in Mbyá-Guaraní thought the soul itself is a divine word. The sacred creation chants are called Ayvu Rapyta, the foundation of human speech.

NAMES.m: Wisdom, knowledge gathered through the seasons
NAMES.i: Arandu joins ara (time) with the idea of listening, so wisdom is what time teaches those who listen. It is a respected word among Guaraní elders and is used as a given name today.

NAMES.m: Sun, bright source of warmth and life
NAMES.i: Kuarahy is the Guaraní word for the sun, which gives life to the maize fields and forests. It is a bright, strong name for a boy and is increasingly chosen by families reclaiming Guaraní heritage.

NAMES.m: Creator, first light who shaped the world
NAMES.i: In Mbyá-Guaraní cosmology Ñamandu is the first father, who rose from darkness with the sun's light and created the first words and the earth's first beings. The name is used by Mbyá families as an honor to the creator.

NAMES.m: Bird, free wanderer of sky and canopy
NAMES.i: Guyra means bird, a creature the Guaraní hold sacred as a messenger between earth and sky. The word appears in many names of birds and places in Paraguay, such as Guyra Campana, the bellbird.

NAMES.m: Divine thunder, spirit of sky and storm
NAMES.i: Tupã is the Tupi-Guaraní name for the divine power heard in thunder and rain. Missionaries later used it for the Christian God, and it remains a respected given name in Brazil and Paraguay.

Lautaro is the Hispanized form of Leftraru, from lef (swift) and traru (the crested caracara). Leftraru was the 16th-century Mapuche toqui who learned Spanish tactics and became a lasting symbol of Mapuche courage and freedom.

NAMES.m: Jaguar of the mountain forest, a guardian spirit
NAMES.i: Nawel is the Mapudungun word for the jaguar or great cat of the Andean forests. It is prized as a protective force, and Lake Nahuel Huapi in Patagonia takes its name from it, meaning 'island of the jaguar'.

NAMES.m: Sun, giver of warmth and the day
NAMES.i: Antü is the sun in Mapudungun. In Mapuche cosmology it is honored in ceremonies such as the We Tripantu, the new year celebrated at the winter solstice when the sun begins its return.
NAMES.src: Mapuche oral tradition; We Tripantu ceremony

NAMES.m: Moon, silver lamp of the night sky
NAMES.i: Küyen is the moon, which the Mapuche use to count the months and to guide planting and ceremony. It is often paired with Antü, the sun, in the Mapuche vision of a balanced world.

NAMES.m: Golden flower, a blossom of gold
NAMES.i: Millaray joins milla (gold) with rayen (flower). It evokes a bloom that gleams in the sun, and it is a well-loved Mapuche girl's name in Chile today.

NAMES.m: Flower, a blossom opening to spring
NAMES.i: Rayen is the Mapudungun word for flower. It is one of the most loved Mapuche names for girls, and it appears in compounds such as Millaray (golden flower) and Rayenray.

NAMES.m: Dawn, the first light of morning
NAMES.i: Liwen means morning or daybreak in Mapudungun. It names the hour of fresh light when families rise and ceremonies often begin.

NAMES.m: Blue, the color of sky and sacred stone
NAMES.i: Kallfü means blue in Mapudungun, a color tied to the sky and to sacred things. It is the root of the Mapuche leader's name Kallfükura, 'blue stone', better known as Calfucurá, the 19th-century lonko.

NAMES.m: River, a flowing and living water
NAMES.i: Leufü is the Mapudungun word for river. Rivers are the veins of the Mapuche homeland, the Wallmapu, and are held to carry the spirit of the land (ngen) within their waters.
Aylén is a modern Mapuche-derived name linked to ayen (laughter) and ayüwün (joy). It is popular in Chile and Argentina, where it is understood as a cheerful, light-hearted name.

NAMES.m: Fragrant forest vine, woven for honor and blessing
NAMES.i: Maile is a sweet-scented native vine whose leaves are twisted into the open-ended maile lei. It is worn at weddings, openings and treaties of peace. In hula tradition it is gathered from the forest as an offering to Laka, goddess of the dance.

The delicate ilima blossom is the flower of Oʻahu. Its golden-orange petals were strung into lei for Hawaiian aliʻi, and it took hundreds of blossoms to make a single strand. The name evokes quiet nobility and a gentle glow.

NAMES.m: Crimson ʻōhiʻa blossom, flower of faithful love
NAMES.i: In the legend of Ōhiʻa and Lehua, the goddess Pele desired the handsome Ōhiʻa, but he was devoted to Lehua. Pele turned him into a gnarled tree, and the other gods turned Lehua into a blossom on his branches so the lovers would never be parted.
NAMES.src: Hawaiian legend of Ōhiʻa and Lehua

NAMES.m: Rainbow, bridge between the earth and the gods
NAMES.i: The rainbow was a sacred sign in Hawaiʻi, a pathway for gods and spirits and a mark of chiefly presence. In some traditions Anuenue is the rainbow maiden who carries messages between the heavens and the earth.

Hiʻiakaikapoliopele, 'Hiʻiaka in the bosom of Pele', is the favorite youngest sister of the volcano goddess. She is a healer and a patron of hula. In the great epic she crosses the islands to fetch Pele's lover, faithful and courageous throughout.
NAMES.src: Epic of Hiʻiaka, Hawaiian oral tradition

NAMES.m: Orange tree, sweet with fragrance and awakening
NAMES.i: Alani is the Hawaiian word for the orange tree and its fragrant fruit. It also suggests waking, as in the freshness of morning. It is a bright, sweet name that was adopted into the language and taken to heart.

NAMES.m: Heavenly flower, blossom from the sky
NAMES.i: Pua is blossom and lani is heaven. The name describes a child as a flower sent from the sky, and it appears often in Hawaiian songs and chants that praise beloved women and beloved places.

NAMES.m: Song or chant, the voice of memory
NAMES.i: Mele is any Hawaiian song, poem or chant. Before writing, Hawaiian history, genealogy and the creation story of the Kumulipo were kept alive through mele, memorized and passed from teacher to student.

NAMES.m: Wave, rolling surf of the open sea
NAMES.i: Nalu means wave or surf, and also something that flows. Surfing, heʻe nalu, was an ancient Hawaiian art enjoyed by chiefs and commoners and surrounded by chants and rituals.

NAMES.m: Koa tree, symbol of courage and bold heart
NAMES.i: Koa is the tall native hardwood from which canoes were carved, and the word also means brave. The tree carried voyagers across the open ocean, and its name stands for courage that is steady and protective.

NAMES.m: Clever demigod who pulled islands from the sea
NAMES.i: Māui is the trickster-hero of Polynesian tradition. In Hawaiian lore he hauls up the islands with his magic fishhook and slows the sun on Haleakalā so that his mother's bark cloth can dry.

NAMES.m: God of rain, harvest, music and peace
NAMES.i: Lono is the god of thunderclouds, fertile rain, agriculture and music. During the Makahiki season, a time of peace, feasting and games, his banner traveled around the island.

NAMES.m: Free one, spirit unbound and open as the sea
NAMES.i: Kanoa means 'the free one'. It has long been a favorite name in Hawaiian families, hoping for a child whose spirit is generous and unconfined.

NAMES.m: Strength, steady power of body and spirit
NAMES.i: Ikaika is strength, vigor and resilience. It names the endurance that moves a voyager across open water and a family through hardship, and it is rooted in the strong, the stable and the enduring.

NAMES.m: Ocean maiden, spirit of the sea
NAMES.i: Hinemoana is the personified ocean, a woman of the sea whose moods are the tides and waves. Coastal iwi remember her as the wide blue breath surrounding Aotearoa.

NAMES.m: Maiden of the waters and the soft mist
NAMES.i: Hinewai joins hine (girl, maiden) with wai (fresh water). She is the spirit of streams and mist on the hills, a name that sounds like rain on leaves.

NAMES.m: Peace, calm sky, and quiet heart
NAMES.i: Rangimarie joins rangi (sky) with marie (calm), the stillness of a clear day. It is a name of peace often given in hope for a gentle life.

NAMES.m: Blossom opening like a spring flower
NAMES.i: Puawai means a flower in bloom, and the name is used as a metaphor for a flourishing child. Pua (flower) and wai (water) suggest a blossom nourished by water.

NAMES.m: Dawn, broad daylight after the night
NAMES.i: Awatea names full daylight, the moment the world is revealed after Te Pō, the night. It carries the hope of a bright beginning.

NAMES.m: Treasure, precious jewel of the blue sky
NAMES.i: Kahurangi means a treasured person or thing, and also a prized, translucent variety of pounamu (greenstone). It is a name for a cherished child, and Kahurangi National Park carries it too.

NAMES.m: Good fortune and still, peaceful water
NAMES.i: Waimarie means luck or good fortune. Its parts, wai (water) and marie (calm), suggest still water, a good sign of safe passage.

NAMES.m: Brave, confident, and bold of spirit
NAMES.i: In te reo Māori, maia means courageous and self-assured. It was used in praise of those who face the unknown, such as voyagers and orators.
Ataahua describes beauty of person, landscape, or deed. Its first part, ata, means dawn or morning, so beauty is imagined as the early light.

NAMES.m: Man, and lord of the forest and its light
NAMES.i: Tāne Mahuta, god of forests and birds, pushed apart his parents Ranginui and Papatūānuku to let light enter the world. The great kauri Tāne Mahuta in Waipoua Forest carries his name.
Tūtānekai lived on Mokoia Island in Lake Rotorua and played his flute in the evenings. The music drew Hinemoa across the water to him.

NAMES.m: Clever hero who fished up islands
NAMES.i: Māui, the youngest and cleverest of his brothers, slowed the sun with a noose so people had longer days. He also hauled Te Ika-a-Māui, the North Island, from the sea with a magic fishhook.

NAMES.m: Voyager who first found the long white cloud
NAMES.i: Kupe sailed from Hawaiki in his canoe Matahourua and is credited with first reaching Aotearoa. His wife Kuramārōtini is said to have named it from the cloud on the horizon.

NAMES.m: Crimson-flowering forest tree and legendary canoe-builder
NAMES.i: Rātā is a tree that blooms crimson in the forest. In legend Rātā felled a tree for his canoe without proper karakia, and the forest spirits and birds raised it up again. The lesson is respect for the forest.

Aoraki was a son of Rakinui the sky father. When his canoe was wrecked, he and his brothers turned to stone, and he became the highest peak of the Southern Alps. The mountain is an ancestor of Ngāi Tahu.

NAMES.m: Peace-bringer and god of cultivated food
NAMES.i: Rongo, or Rongo-mā-Tāne, is the atua of cultivated crops such as kūmara, and also of peace. Gardens and marae both honour him.

NAMES.m: Sky wind, the stirring of weather
NAMES.i: Tāwhiri is a short form of Tāwhirimātea, atua of wind, clouds, and storms. He stayed with his father Ranginui when the other children separated their parents, and his winds still move over the earth.
Ranginui is the sky father, who lay in embrace with Papatūānuku the earth mother until their children parted them. His tears fall as rain, and the dew is said to be his love for her.

NAMES.m: Tide, the rising and falling sea
NAMES.i: Tai means the sea, the coast, or the tide. It appears in many place names and in iwi names such as Ngāi Tahu, and it suits a child tied to the shore.

NAMES.m: Star cluster of the Māori New Year
NAMES.i: Matariki is the Pleiades, whose rising in midwinter marks the start of the Māori new year. Families gather to remember the dead, give thanks, and plant hopes for the season ahead.

NAMES.m: Star, a shining light in the night sky
NAMES.i: Whetū is the star, used by navigators to find their way across the Pacific. As a name it means a guiding light.

NAMES.m: Swift falcon of the high forest skies
NAMES.i: The kārearea is Aotearoa's native falcon, a fast and fearless hunter of the forest edge and high country. The name gives a child its speed, sharp sight, and independence.

NAMES.m: Sacred fire, radiant son of Ahura Mazda
NAMES.i: In the Avesta, Atar is the living fire, called the son of Ahura Mazda. He stands as the visible sign of truth, and Zoroastrians pray before his flame in every fire temple. His light is held to be pure enough to carry human prayers upward.

NAMES.m: Truth, the radiant order of the cosmos
NAMES.i: Asha is the central Zoroastrian principle of truth, righteousness and cosmic harmony, set against the Lie (druj). Asha Vahishta, 'Best Truth', is one of the Amesha Spentas and is tied to fire. Whoever lives by asha keeps the world in tune.

NAMES.m: Good thought, a mind turned toward the light
NAMES.i: Vohu Manah, 'Good Mind', is the first of the Amesha Spentas, the holy immortals around Ahura Mazda. In the Gathas, Zarathustra meets Ahura Mazda through this radiant being. Vohu Manah also watches over cattle and the gentle side of creation.

NAMES.m: Devotion, gentle harmony of the fertile earth
NAMES.i: Spenta Armaiti, 'Holy Devotion', is the Amesha Spenta of earth and humble piety. She is the daughter of Ahura Mazda in the Gathas, and the green world answers to her. In later Persian tradition she became Spandarmad and gave her name to a month.

NAMES.m: Wholeness, the perfect flow of water and health
NAMES.i: Haurvatat means wholeness or perfection. She is the Amesha Spenta who guards water and health, and she is paired with Ameretat. Together they bring abundance to those who follow truth.

NAMES.m: Immortality, the undying bloom of plants
NAMES.i: Ameretat, 'Deathlessness', is the Amesha Spenta who protects plants and the promise of eternal life. She and Haurvatat are the twin gifts Ahura Mazda gives the faithful. Persian tradition remembers her in the month and festival of Mordad.

NAMES.m: Dawn, golden herald of the returning sun
NAMES.i: Ushah is the Avestan dawn, one of the guardian powers of the five divisions of the day. She belongs to the Indo-Iranian heritage of the dawn goddess that Vedic Ushas also shares. Each morning she opens the sky to the light of Mithra and the sun.

NAMES.m: Covenant of light, guardian of truth and friendship
NAMES.i: Mithra is the Yazata of covenants, friendship and sunrise. In Yasht 10 he rides across the land before the sun with a thousand ears and ten thousand eyes, seeing every promise kept or broken. His name later traveled across the Roman world as Mithras.

NAMES.m: Victory, the triumphant breaking of obstacles
NAMES.i: Verethragna is the Yazata of victory, who appears in Yasht 14 in ten forms, among them wind, bull, white horse, boar and falcon. His name means 'smiting of resistance'. It lives on as Bahram, a name borne by Persian kings.

NAMES.m: Shining star, rain-bringer of the sky
NAMES.i: Tishtrya is the star Sirius, who in Yasht 8 fights the drought-demon Apaosha in the form of a white horse. When the faithful honor him, he floods the world with rain and refills the sea. He is the bright guardian of the harvest.

NAMES.m: Radiant sun, the swift-horsed shining one
NAMES.i: Hvare Khshaeta, 'Radiant Sun', is the Yazata of the sun, honored in Yasht 6 as the one who cleanses the world with light. He is called swift-horsed and is invoked with Mithra. The modern Persian Khorshid grew from this name.

NAMES.m: Moon, silver keeper of the seeds of cattle
NAMES.i: Mah is the Avestan moon, honored in Yasht 7 as the keeper of the seed of the primordial bull from which animal life came. Zoroastrians greet each new moon with prayers of gratitude. The name remains the Persian word for both moon and month.

NAMES.m: Inner vision, the luminous conscience of the soul
NAMES.i: Daena is the inner vision or conscience that meets each soul at the Chinvat Bridge. The righteous see her as a radiant, beautiful maiden who guides them across. The word also came to mean 'religion' and gave Persian its word din.

NAMES.m: Blessing, radiant goddess of fortune and reward
NAMES.i: Ashi Vanguhi, 'Good Reward', is the Yazata of fortune, abundance and just recompense, praised in Yasht 17. She is the daughter of Ahura Mazda and sister of Sraosha and Mithra. She blesses homes with children and prosperity.

NAMES.m: Just judge, the steady scales of truth
NAMES.i: Rashnu is the Yazata of justice, praised in Yasht 12 (Rashn Yasht). He weighs the deeds of the dead on his golden scales at the Chinvat Bridge. His judgment is perfectly fair and cannot be bribed.

NAMES.m: Listening, the watchful guardian who heeds the divine
NAMES.i: Sraosha, 'Attentive Hearing' or 'Obedience', is the Yazata who guards the world from demons through the night. He is the first to pray and the helper of souls on the three nights after death. Persian Sorush comes from his name.

NAMES.m: Abundant insight, the wise and clear-sighted one
NAMES.i: Pouruchista was the youngest daughter of Zarathustra and Hvovi. Her name means 'rich in insight'. She is remembered as a wise woman whom her father asked to settle a debate on faith, and she is honored as a model of devotion.

NAMES.m: Holy bounty, a gift that grows and gives
NAMES.i: Spenta means holy, bounteous or life-giving. It is the epithet of the Amesha Spentas and of Spenta Mainyu, the Bounteous Spirit of Ahura Mazda. In the Gathas it names the generous power that makes creation flourish.

NAMES.m: Friend, the healing companion of the community
NAMES.i: Airyaman is the Yazata of friendship, kinship and healing. The Airyaman Ishya prayer asks that his desired fellowship come to help the followers of Zarathustra. His name lives on in the word Iran, from the Aryans, 'the noble ones'.

From the root mery, 'beloved', this is a common element in Egyptian names. Merit was also the name of a goddess who gave order to song and ritual, and of many women whose families wanted them cherished.
NAMES.src: Old and Middle Kingdom personal names; Pyramid Texts epithets

NAMES.m: Throne, queen of heaven and mother of Horus
NAMES.i: This is the Egyptian name of Isis, whose hieroglyph is a throne. She gathered the scattered body of Osiris and, with her wings, breathed life back into him. Egyptians saw in her the devoted wife and mother, and a source of magic.
NAMES.src: Pyramid Texts (c. 2400 BCE); Book of the Dead

NAMES.m: Moisture of heaven, goddess of dew and rain
NAMES.i: Tefnut is the sister and consort of Shu, the air, and was born from the sun god's own breath. In myth she left Egypt in anger, and the land dried up. Her return brought back the green of the fields.

NAMES.m: She who lives for Amun, giver of breath
NAMES.i: Daughter of Nefertiti and Akhenaten, she became the wife of the young Tutankhamun. Born Ankhesenpaaten, she changed her name when the old gods were restored. Her name begins with ankh, the sign of life.

NAMES.m: Child born of Ra, son of the sun
NAMES.i: Ra-mes-su means 'Ra has fashioned him', the name taken by the Ramesside kings. Ramose was also the name of a vizier under Amenhotep III and IV, whose tomb at Thebes has reliefs in a refined style.

NAMES.m: Child of the moon, born of Iah
NAMES.i: Ahmose I drove the Hyksos out of Egypt and founded the Eighteenth Dynasty, opening the New Kingdom. His name links him to Iah, the moon god, whose silver light the Egyptians used to mark the months.
NAMES.src: Biography of Ahmose son of Ibana, Eileithyia (c. 1500 BCE)

NAMES.m: Traveler of the night sky, moon healer
NAMES.i: Khonsu, son of Amun and Mut, crosses the sky each night as the moon, and his name means 'the traveler'. He was a god of healing, and the Bentresh Stela tells of his statue sent abroad to cure a foreign princess.
NAMES.src: Pyramid Texts; Bentresh Stela; Karnak temple inscriptions

NAMES.m: Rising sun, the scarab of becoming
NAMES.i: Khepri, whose name means 'he who comes into being', is the sun at dawn, a scarab beetle rolling the disk over the horizon. Egyptians saw in the dung beetle's ball a model of rebirth.
NAMES.src: Book of the Dead; Pyramid Texts (c. 2400 BCE)

NAMES.m: One who comes in peace, sage and healer
NAMES.i: Imhotep served King Djoser and is credited with designing the Step Pyramid at Saqqara, the first great stone building. Egyptians later honored him as a god of healing and wisdom.
NAMES.src: Step Pyramid at Saqqara base inscription (c. 2650 BCE); later Wisdom tradition

NAMES.m: Falcon of the heights, the one on high
NAMES.i: This is the Egyptian form of Horus. As a falcon-headed god, his right eye was the sun and his left the moon. He grew up in the marshes of the Delta, hidden by Isis, and won back the throne of his father Osiris.
NAMES.src: Pyramid Texts (c. 2400 BCE); Contendings of Horus and Seth

NAMES.m: Lord of the green fields, the risen one
NAMES.i: Asar is the Egyptian form of Osiris, the green-skinned king who was killed, restored by Isis, and became ruler of the afterlife. The Nile's yearly flood and the sprouting of grain were seen as his return.
NAMES.src: Pyramid Texts (c. 2400 BCE); Book of the Dead

NAMES.m: Peace of Amun, the hidden one is content
NAMES.i: Four pharaohs of the Eighteenth Dynasty bore this name, and Amenhotep III ruled during a time of great wealth and monuments. Hotep means peace, offering, and satisfaction, all joined in one word.

Nakht means 'strong' and was borne by scribes and officials. In the Theban tomb of Nakht, an astronomer-scribe of Amun, painted scenes show harvesting, fowling in the marshes, and a musician playing the harp.

NAMES.m: Moon, silver lamp of the night
NAMES.i: Iah is the Egyptian word and god of the moon, often shown with a crescent holding a full disk. Egyptians counted months by his phases, and the name appears within others such as Ahmose.
NAMES.src: Pyramid Texts (c. 2400 BCE); Book of the Dead

NAMES.m: Hero who sought eternal life and returned wise
NAMES.i: Gilgamesh, king of Uruk, felled the great cedars of the Forest with his friend Enkidu and journeyed to the ends of the earth seeking immortality. He returned having learned that his lasting legacy would be the walls and stories he left behind. The Sumerian form of the name is Bilgames.
NAMES.src: Epic of Gilgamesh (Standard Babylonian, c. 1200 BCE; Sumerian poems c. 2100 BCE)

NAMES.m: Radiant sun, bringer of daylight and justice
NAMES.i: Utu was the Sumerian sun god, who rose each morning from the mountains and judged fairly in the light of day. He helped Gilgamesh on the road to the cedar forest by sending storm winds against the guardian Humbaba.
NAMES.src: Sumerian Gilgamesh poems; Sumerian king and god lists

NAMES.m: Great lady, moon-queen of the reed marshes
NAMES.i: Ningal, 'Great Lady,' was the wife of the moon god Nanna and the mother of Inanna and Utu. In 'The Lament for Ur' she grieves for her city, a haunting scene that has made her a symbol of tenderness and faithful sorrow.
NAMES.src: Lament for Ur (c. 2000 BCE); hymns to Nanna

NAMES.m: Faithful son, shepherd beloved of heaven's queen
NAMES.i: Dumuzi, from dumu-zi, 'faithful son,' was the shepherd-king beloved by Inanna. Sumerian love songs speak of him bringing cream and milk to his bride, and his yearly return is tied to spring's renewal.
NAMES.src: Inanna and Dumuzi love songs (c. 2000 BCE); Descent of Inanna

NAMES.m: Vine of heaven, devoted sister and singer
NAMES.i: Geshtinanna, whose name means 'Heaven's Grapevine,' was the sister of Dumuzi. She was a poet and interpreter of dreams, and she offered to spend half of each year in the underworld in his place.
NAMES.src: Dumuzi's Dream; Descent of Inanna (c. 2000 BCE)

NAMES.m: Lady of the red light of heaven, the star Venus
NAMES.i: Ninsianna is a Sumerian name for Inanna as the planet Venus, the bright red-gold star seen near the horizon at dawn and dusk. Temple astronomers recorded her risings and settings as sacred signs.
NAMES.src: Sumerian astral hymns; Venus tablet traditions (c. 2000 BCE)

NAMES.m: Lady of the waters, guardian of the poor and prophetess
NAMES.i: Nanshe was the goddess of the marshlands and fisheries near the Gulf, and a divine interpreter of dreams. She protected orphans and widows, and each New Year she judged the conduct of humankind with fairness.
NAMES.src: Hymn to Nanshe (c. 2100 BCE); Gudea cylinders

NAMES.m: Lady of the open air and gentle breezes
NAMES.i: Ninlil was the goddess of the winds and the grain, wife of the air-god Enlil. In the myth of 'Enlil and Ninlil,' she walks by the canal at Nippur and her story becomes a tale of devotion and the birth of the moon god.

NAMES.m: Finder of life everlasting, survivor of the flood
NAMES.i: Ziusudra, 'He Who Saw Life of Long Days,' was the pious king who survived the great flood in a boat. The gods rewarded him with eternal life in the land of Dilmun, and he is the Sumerian forerunner of Noah and of Utnapishtim, whom Gilgamesh visits.
NAMES.src: Eridu Genesis (c. 1600 BCE); Sumerian flood tradition

NAMES.m: Young king, swift and gentle companion of the mountain
NAMES.i: Lugalbanda was a legendary king of Uruk and the father of Gilgamesh. In the epic tale 'Lugalbanda in the Mountain Cave,' he is left ill in the wilderness, is aided by the gods, and wins the favor of the Anzu bird, who grants him swiftness.
NAMES.src: Lugalbanda epics (c. 2100 BCE); Sumerian King List

NAMES.m: Wise queen, steadfast counselor of the steppe
NAMES.i: Kanykei is the clear-sighted wife of Manas, said to be a princess from Bukhara. In the epic she guides him with foresight and protects his household and his son Semetey after he dies.
Aichurek is the wife of Semetey in the Kyrgyz epic cycle, known for her magical gifts and moonlike beauty. The name joins ai, 'moon,' with a word for radiance or heart.
NAMES.src: Epic of Manas, Semetey cycle (oral tradition)

NAMES.m: Loyal companion, praised friend of the hero
NAMES.i: Almambet is a famed warrior of Chinese-Kalmyk origin who becomes Manas's closest ally and sworn brother. His story is one of friendship that crosses borders. The name is a Kyrgyz form of Muhammad.

NAMES.m: Wise elder, watchful guardian of the people
NAMES.i: Bakai is the sage counselor of Manas, a gray-bearded advisor whose foresight keeps the Kyrgyz coalition together. He stands for the elder whose word steadies the young hero.
Kökchö is one of the forty champions who ride with Manas, remembered for wisdom as well as courage. His name comes from kök, the Turkic word for 'blue' and 'sky.'

NAMES.m: Young hero of the third generation, restorer of glory
NAMES.i: Seytek is the grandson of Manas and the hero of the third part of the trilogy. He avenges his family and brings the Kyrgyz lands back to peace. His name closes the epic's arc across three generations.
NAMES.src: Epic of Manas, Seytek cycle (oral tradition)

NAMES.m: Golden eagle, sovereign of the high mountains
NAMES.i: Burkut is the golden eagle, the bird Kyrgyz hunters, called berkutchu, have trained for centuries. In the epic tradition the eagle is a symbol of courage, keen sight, and the free spirit of the steppe.
NAMES.src: Kyrgyz oral tradition; eagle imagery in the Manas epic

NAMES.m: Morning star, bright herald of the dawn
NAMES.i: Cholpon is the Turkic name for Venus, the morning star that rises before the sun over Lake Issyk-Kul. It gives its name to the lakeside town of Cholpon-Ata, 'father of the morning star.'

NAMES.m: Star shining over the night steppe
NAMES.i: Jyldyz means 'star' in Kyrgyz. For nomads crossing the steppe, the night sky was a map, and stars guided herders and riders home.
Aruuke comes from aruu, 'pure' or 'beautiful,' with an endearing suffix. It belongs to the Kyrgyz tradition of praising girls as clear as mountain water and as bright as snow.
Aigul joins ai, 'moon,' and gül, 'flower.' It is a loved Turkic name that evokes a pale blossom opening under moonlight in the high meadows (jailoo) of the Tian Shan.

NAMES.m: Brave hero of the underworld journey
NAMES.i: Er Töshtük is the hero of a Kyrgyz epic that sits beside the Manas cycle in oral tradition. He descends into the underworld, faces its giants, and returns carrying wisdom. Here the warrior's courage is joined to a journey of discovery.

NAMES.m: Dragon maiden, radiant queen of Ling
NAMES.i: Drugmo is the beloved wife of King Gesar in the Ling epic. She is known for her beauty and loyalty, and her name carries the thunder-dragon of the Tibetan sky.

Dolma is the Tibetan name of Tara, the Buddhist goddess who is said to have been born from a tear of Avalokiteshvara's compassion. Tibetans call on her to cross safely over fear and danger. It is one of the most beloved names for Tibetan girls.

NAMES.m: Lotus, purity blooming from the mud
NAMES.i: Pema is the Tibetan form of the Sanskrit padma, the lotus that rises unstained from muddy water. It recalls Padmasambhava, the Lotus-Born master who carried Buddhism across the Himalayas.

NAMES.m: Holder of the teachings, keeper of the dharma
NAMES.i: Tenzin joins 'tenpa' (teaching) with 'dzin' (to hold). It is the monastic name given to the Fourteenth Dalai Lama, Tenzin Gyatso, and to many Tibetan children.

NAMES.m: Moon, silver lamp of the Himalayan night
NAMES.i: Dawa is the Tibetan word for moon and also the name for Monday. Children born on that day are often given it, and the moon's cool light is a classic image of the calm mind.

NAMES.m: Sun, golden light over the snow peaks
NAMES.i: Nyima means sun and is the name for Sunday. Tibetans give it to children born on that day, and it evokes the first light striking the glaciers at dawn.

NAMES.m: Great bliss, deep and lasting happiness
NAMES.i: Dechen means great bliss, the joy of awakened mind in Buddhist teaching. It is also the name of Dewachen, the Pure Land of Amitabha. It is a gentle name for girls and for boys.

NAMES.m: Melodious one, goddess of song and speech
NAMES.i: Yangchenma, 'the one with melody,' is the Tibetan name for Sarasvati, the goddess of music, speech and learning. Her name is given to girls in the hope of a sweet voice and a clear mind.

NAMES.m: Gentle melody, voice of soft wisdom
NAMES.i: Jamyang is the Tibetan name of Manjushri, the bodhisattva of wisdom, who holds a flaming sword that cuts through ignorance. The name joins 'gentle' with 'melodious voice,' as wisdom spoken softly.

Dorje is the Tibetan form of vajra, the diamond-hard thunderbolt that stands for indestructible wisdom. Tantric masters hold it as a ritual scepter, and Tibetan families give the name to boys as a blessing of strength.

NAMES.m: Flower, bloom of the high meadow
NAMES.i: Metok is the Tibetan word for flower. It appears in names such as Metok Lhamo, and it recalls the brief summer meadows of the plateau, covered in blue poppies and primulas. It was used in offerings and poetry long before it became a name.

NAMES.m: Lady-blossom, a radiant flower of the steppe
NAMES.i: Banu Çiçek is the beautiful, quick-witted heroine of the tale of Bamsı Beyrek in the Book of Dede Korkut. She wins her betrothed through a contest of horse-riding, archery and wrestling, then keeps faith with him through sixteen years of his captivity.
NAMES.src: Book of Dede Korkut (15th c. manuscripts)

NAMES.m: Young bull, steadfast prince of the Oghuz
NAMES.i: Boğaç Khan is the hero of the first tale in the Book of Dede Korkut. As a boy he is named by Dede Korkut himself after he defeats a wild bull, and the name carries the steppe's admiration for noble strength.
NAMES.src: Book of Dede Korkut (15th c. manuscripts)

NAMES.m: Moonlight, the luminous halo around the moon
NAMES.i: Ayla comes from the Turkish ay, 'moon,' which has been sacred in Turkic poetry and steppe imagery since ancient times. It evokes the silver ring of light that gathers around the moon on a clear night.

NAMES.m: Luminous one, enlightened as the moonlit sky
NAMES.i: Aydın is built from ay, 'moon,' and means bright, clear and enlightened. In Turkish it is both a name and a word for an educated, illuminated mind.

NAMES.m: Sky-blue grace, fair as the heavens
NAMES.i: Gökçe comes from gök, the 'sky,' sacred in Turkic belief as Gök Tengri, the Blue Sky. As a name it means 'heavenly' or 'sky-like,' and in Turkish poetry it also praises a person's beauty.

NAMES.m: River, a flowing stream carrying the steppe's song
NAMES.i: Irmak is the Turkish word for 'river.' Rivers such as the Amu Darya and the Syr Darya shaped the migrations and memory of the Turkic peoples as they moved west from Central Asia.

NAMES.m: Noble falcon soaring high above the steppe
NAMES.i: Togan is an old Turkic word for a trained hunting falcon, a bird prized by khans and nomad hunters across the steppe. Falconry was a mark of nobility, and the name carries the image of a keen, free spirit in flight.

NAMES.m: Falcon of noble flight, a king among birds
NAMES.i: Tuğrul (Tughril) means a bird of prey, often rendered as falcon. It was borne by Tuğrul Bey, founder of the Seljuk dynasty, whose Oghuz warriors carried Turkic culture across Persia and into Anatolia.

NAMES.m: Bard, minstrel of the kopuz and keeper of tales
NAMES.i: Ozan is the old Turkic word for the minstrel-poet who sang epics to the kopuz. The Book of Dede Korkut honors Dede Korkut himself as the supreme ozan of the Oghuz.
NAMES.src: Book of Dede Korkut (15th c. manuscripts)

NAMES.m: Sun and moon together, a radiant princess
NAMES.i: Mihrimah joins the Persian mihr, 'sun,' and mah, 'moon.' It was the name of Mihrimah Sultan, daughter of Suleiman the Magnificent, whose mosques in Istanbul are known for their light.

NAMES.m: Wise counselor, sage of clear understanding
NAMES.i: Bilge is an Old Turkic word for wisdom, borne in the 8th century by Bilge Khagan, whose memorial inscriptions urge his people toward unity and good rule. As a given name it suits a child of thoughtful insight.
NAMES.src: Orkhon inscriptions (8th c. CE); Turkic tradition
